ApostropheCMS CVE-2026-53609 prototype-pollution poisoning via $pullAll __proto__ AIExploitation High
Hunts the exploitation request for CVE-2026-53609: an authenticated-editor PATCH to an ApostropheCMS piece-type REST endpoint whose body carries a prototype-pollution key (__proto__ / $pullAll / publicApiProjection). This is the one poisoning request that permanently disables authorization for the whole Node.js process, so catching the payload itself is the highest-fidelity pivot. Rationale: Uses the exact article strings: PATCH method, the /api/v1/@apostrophecms/ piece-type path, and the pollution tokens __proto__/$pullAll/publicApiProjection (plus URL-encoded %5F%5Fproto%5F%5F). Cross-checked against the GHSA advisory, TheHackerWire and OffSeq write-ups confirming the $pullAll/__proto__ vector and publicApiProjection gadget. Body inspection depends on WAF/proxy telemetry, hence CommonSecurityLog rather than endpoint EDR. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6h5j-32cf-4253 • https://www.thehackerwire.com/apostrophecms-critical-prototype-pollution-leads-to-auth-bypass/ • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-53609-cwe-1321-improperly-controlled-modi-874d30d1
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate editor PATCH to a global/piece doc whose content JSON legitimately contains a field literally named 'constructor' or 'prototype'
  • Security scanners (Burp Suite, OWASP ZAP, Nuclei prototype-pollution templates) probing the endpoint during authorized testing
  • Automated content-migration scripts submitting dot-notation patch keys in bulk
  • WAF-blocked requests that never reached the app (still worth confirming the block held)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceAction !in~ ("blocked","denied","deny","reset") and RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Burp","Nuclei","zap")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the SourceUserName/SourceIP and confirm the request reached the app (2xx) rather than being WAF-blocked; pull the full request body to confirm the __proto__/$pullAll key. 2) Contain: because the pollution persists for the process lifetime, restart the affected Node.js/ApostropheCMS worker processes immediately to clear Object.prototype, revoke the editor session/token used, and virtual-patch the WAF to drop bodies containing __proto__/constructor/prototype keys on piece-type endpoints. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same SourceIP/user for follow-on unauthenticated GETs to /api/v1/@apostrophecms/user and /global (see companion UC) and confirm the CMS is upgraded past 4.30.0.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "PATCH"
| where RequestURL has "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/"
| where RequestURL has_any ("__proto__","%5F%5Fproto%5F%5F","constructor","prototype","$pullAll","publicApiProjection")
    or Message has_any ("__proto__","$pullAll","publicApiProjection")
    or RequestContext has_any ("__proto__","$pullAll","publicApiProjection")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction, Message
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

ApostropheCMS CVE-2026-53609 authorization-bypass aftermath: unauthenticated 200 on protected piece-type API AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the post-exploitation signal of CVE-2026-53609: once Object.prototype.publicApiProjection is poisoned, previously-protected piece-type endpoints (@apostrophecms/user, @apostrophecms/global) return HTTP 200 to unauthenticated requests instead of the normal 404 'notfound'. Surfaces the auth-bypass effect even when the poisoning PATCH body was not logged. Rationale: Encodes the article's observed behavioural flip: /api/v1/@apostrophecms/user returns 'notfound' (404) when unauthenticated but 200 with a paginated result set after the bypass. Filters to GET + 200 + empty auth user on the two verified-affected endpoints (user, global). Corroborated by GHSA and TheHackerWire confirming both endpoints are affected and the bypass serves unauthenticated visitors. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6h5j-32cf-4253 • https://www.thehackerwire.com/apostrophecms-critical-prototype-pollution-leads-to-auth-bypass/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Piece types intentionally configured with publicApiProjection so their API is public by design (content-delivery endpoints)
  • Uptime/health-check monitors polling API paths and receiving 200
  • CsUsername empty because authentication is via Bearer token or session cookie (not basic auth), mislabeling a legitimately authenticated editor as unauthenticated
  • CDN/edge cache serving a previously-cached 200 response for a public content type
Suppression filter
| where CsUriStem has "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the 200 was served to a genuinely unauthenticated caller (no Bearer/cookie) and that the target type — especially @apostrophecms/user — is NOT meant to be public; a public user list is never expected. 2) Contain: restart the ApostropheCMS Node.js worker processes to clear the polluted prototype, then block the offending SourceIP at the WAF and audit what user/global data was returned. 3) Hunt: correlate backwards to the poisoning PATCH (companion UC) from the same host/session, review all piece-type endpoints for anomalous unauthenticated 200s, and confirm the platform is patched above 4.30.0.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CsMethod =~ "GET"
| where CsUriStem has_any ("/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user","/api/v1/@apostrophecms/global")
| where ScStatus == 200
| where isempty(CsUsername)
| summarize Requests=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Endpoints=make_set(CsUriStem, 10) by CIp, UserAgent, CsHost
| sort by LastSeen desc

Atomic Arch AUR loader/stealer known-bad file & process hashes AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution or on-disk presence of the July 2026 AUR (openconnect-sso) two-stage loader and Rust infostealer by their published SHA256/MD5 hashes. Article-specific: these hashes belong to the IFIN-analyzed Atomic Arch campaign redistributed through hijacked AUR package adoptions. Rationale: Uses the four campaign SHA256 hashes plus the MD5 pre-extracted from the article; SHA256 6144d433... is independently confirmed as the Rust stealer binary by The Hacker News and GuardSix, so hash-based matching is high-fidelity with near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/over-400-arch-linux-aur-packages.html • https://guardsix.com/blog/atomic-arch-zombie-package-apocalypse • https://discourse.ifin.network/t/new-aur-attack-prompts-adoption-lock/698
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst detonating the sample in an authorized sandbox that reports to production EDR
  • Threat-intel/VirusTotal retrohunt downloads of the sample onto a research host
  • Incident-response tooling copying the artifact for evidence collection
  • Backup/AV quarantine re-scanning a previously captured copy
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("clamscan","freshclam","vt","virustotal") and FolderPath !has "/quarantine/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is Arch/Arch-based and whether any AUR package (openconnect-sso, boringssl-git, icloudpd, windscribe-cli-v2-bin, stirling-pdf-desktop-bin, pgadmin4-server) was recently installed/updated via makepkg. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the matching PID, and treat all local secrets (SSH keys, browser creds, cloud/dev/AI tokens) as compromised. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for the disguised dbus-daemon Tor process, systemd units with Restart=always, and cron entries; rotate SSH keys and check known_hosts targets for lateral spread.

Tor client masquerading as dbus-daemon making external network connections AICommand & Control High
Hunts the Atomic Arch first-stage behaviour of launching a Tor client renamed to 'dbus-daemon' to reach an .onion C2. A legitimate dbus-daemon is a local IPC bus and never initiates public/internet egress, so any outbound public connection from a dbus-daemon process is high-fidelity. Rationale: Article states the loader 'downloads and launches a Tor client disguised as dbus-daemon' to reach an .onion server; corroborated by GuardSix noting C2 via a Tor onion service. dbus-daemon making public egress (Defender/Falcon) or running outside /usr/bin (Sentinel/Datadog/Sigma) is essentially never legitimate. Cross-checked against: • https://guardsix.com/blog/atomic-arch-zombie-package-apocalypse • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/over-400-arch-linux-aur-packages.html
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1036.005 T1573.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom-built dbus deployed to a non-standard prefix (/usr/local/bin) on developer boxes — path variant only
  • D-Bus remote/TCP transport intentionally configured in a container or CI runner
  • Chaos/network-testing tooling renamed to system binaries during red-team exercises
  • Flatpak/snap sandboxes shipping their own dbus-daemon under /app or /snap paths
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !in~ ("/usr/bin","/usr/local/bin") or RemotePort in (9001, 9030, 9050, 443)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full path, hash, and command line of the dbus-daemon process; a real one lives at /usr/bin/dbus-daemon and only talks to unix sockets — confirm the destination IP/port and whether it looks like a Tor guard node (443/9001). 2) Contain: isolate the host and kill the process; block the destination IP at egress. 3) Hunt: locate the parent AUR build (makepkg), the second-stage stealer under /var/lib or ~/.config, and any systemd/cron persistence; rotate all secrets on the host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "dbus-daemon"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), Connections = count(), Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 10), RemoteIPs = make_set(RemoteIP, 25) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "dbus-daemon"
| where TargetProcessName !has "/usr/bin/dbus-daemon"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Non-package-manager process writing systemd unit or cron persistence (Atomic Arch) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the loader's persistence step: writing a systemd service (Restart=always) to /etc/systemd/system or ~/.config/systemd/user, plus cron jobs, from a process that is NOT a package manager or systemctl. Article-specific to the AUR loader installing systemd services and cron jobs after anti-analysis checks. Rationale: Article states the loader 'installs systemd services and cron jobs to ensure persistence'; StepSecurity/GuardSix confirm a Restart=always unit dropped to /etc/systemd/system (root) or ~/.config/systemd/user (user). Keying on non-package-manager writers to these exact paths captures the malicious writer while excluding legit installs to /usr/lib/systemd/system. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/400-aur-packages-hijacked-atomic-arch-campaign • https://guardsix.com/blog/atomic-arch-zombie-package-apocalypse
ATT&CKT1543.002 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin hand-authoring a unit with a text editor (vim/nano) or writing crontab via a script
  • Configuration management (Ansible/Chef/Puppet/Salt) deploying systemd units or cron jobs
  • Developer enabling a user service under ~/.config/systemd/user for a legitimate app
  • Container build steps or dotfile-management tools writing unit files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ansible","ansible-playbook","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion","vim","nano","vi","tee") and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","puppet","chef","salt"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the dropped unit/cron file — malicious ones point ExecStart at a binary under /var/lib, ~/.config, /tmp or /dev/shm and use Restart=always; benign ones point at packaged binaries in /usr/bin. 2) Contain: disable/remove the unit or cron entry, kill the referenced binary, and isolate the host if the target is a non-package path. 3) Hunt: pivot to the writing process's ancestry (makepkg build?), check for the disguised dbus-daemon Tor process and stealer artifacts, and rotate host secrets.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.config/systemd/user/","/etc/systemd/system/","/etc/cron.d/","/var/spool/cron/")
| where FileName endswith ".service" or FolderPath has "cron"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("systemctl","systemd","pacman","dpkg","apt","apt-get","rpm","dnf","yum","install","crontab")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRename")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/.config/systemd/user/","/etc/systemd/system/","/etc/cron.d/","/var/spool/cron/")
| where TargetFilePath endswith ".service" or TargetFilePath has "cron"
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("systemctl","systemd","pacman","dpkg","apt","rpm","dnf","crontab"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SSH worm: persistence-path binary spawning ssh/scp for self-propagation AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Atomic Arch stealer's SSH worm capability — a binary running from a malware persistence directory (/var/lib, ~/.config, /tmp, /dev/shm) spawning ssh/scp/sftp/rsync to copy and execute itself on other hosts using stolen SSH keys. Distinguishes malware-driven lateral movement from interactive/administrative SSH. Rationale: Article states the stealer 'can spread laterally by using stolen SSH keys to copy and execute itself on other systems'; corroborated by StepSecurity/HackerNews noting SSH-key and known_hosts theft. Anchoring on ssh/scp spawned by a parent living in the confirmed persistence directories (/var/lib for root, ~/.config for user) targets the worm rather than routine admin SSH. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/over-400-arch-linux-aur-packages.html • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/400-aur-packages-hijacked-atomic-arch-campaign
ATT&CKT1021.004 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom deployment/orchestration scripts installed under /var/lib or a user's ~/.config wrapper that call scp/rsync
  • CI/CD runner or backup agent staged in /tmp or /var/lib performing rsync-over-ssh
  • Developer helper tools in ~/.config invoking git-over-ssh (partly excluded via git filter)
  • Config-management agents copying files to fleet hosts over ssh
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("ansible","rsnapshot","borg","restic","rclone") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gitlab-runner","buildkite-agent","jenkins")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the parent binary's path, hash, and the ssh/scp command line — note the destination host/user and whether a copy of the parent binary is being transferred. 2) Contain: isolate the source host, kill the process, and pre-emptively isolate the destination host(s) named in the command line; revoke/rotate the SSH keys used. 3) Hunt: on each destination host, hunt for the same persistence (systemd Restart=always, cron), the disguised dbus-daemon Tor process, and the campaign hashes; expand outward via known_hosts entries.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("ssh","scp","sftp","rsync")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/var/lib/","/tmp/","/.config/","/dev/shm/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("git","ansible","ansible-playbook","bash","sh","zsh","fish","rsync","ssh","code")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/ssh","/scp","/sftp","/rsync")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/var/lib/","/tmp/","/.config/","/dev/shm/")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("/git","/ansible","/bash","/sh","/zsh","/fish","/rsync","/ssh"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502", "6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b", "42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40") or SHA1 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502", "6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b", "42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40") or MD5 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502", "6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b", "42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502", "6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b", "42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40") or SHA1 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502", "6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b", "42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40") or MD5 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502", "6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b", "42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502", "6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b", "42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Compromised Adform trackpoint-async.js clipper script by SHA256 on endpoint
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Online ad firm Adform’s script compromised to steal cryptocurrency
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] C2 beacon to Adform clipper attacker server 84.32.102.230:7744 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
C2 beacon to Adform clipper attacker server 84.32.102.230:7744 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the attacker-controlled server (84.32.102.230, port 7744) that the trojanized Adform scripts beaconed to, exfiltrating victim IP, referring website and URL path. Any host reaching this IP indicates a browser that loaded the compromised trackpoint-async.js during the July 2026 supply-chain window. Rationale: 84.32.102.230:7744 is the attacker-controlled C2 confirmed in both Beaumont's DoublePulsar analysis and BleepingComputer; it is not owned by Adform and has no benign use, making any connection a high-fidelity indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e • https://www.it-connect.tech/adform-breach-ad-script-steals-cryptocurrency-for-at-least-a-week/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1195.002 T1115
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or malware sandbox intentionally detonating the IOC
  • Threat-intel scanner/crawler validating the C2 from an internal host
  • IP later reassigned to a benign shared-hosting tenant (verify port 7744 and date window July 2026)
  • Corporate VPN/proxy egress IP coincidentally matching (unlikely - it's a /32 attacker host)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host, user and initiating process for the connection; confirm it is a browser (chrome.exe/msedge.exe/firefox.exe) and whether the timestamp falls in the 26-27 July 2026 window. 2) Contain: block 84.32.102.230 at firewall/proxy, and if repeated beaconing is seen, isolate the host and force browser cache/cookie clearing per Adform's guidance. 3) Hunt: pivot to all other hosts that touched this IP, warn affected users to re-verify any crypto wallet addresses they copied/pasted recently, and check for the malicious script hash (see companion UC).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "84.32.102.230"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "84.32.102.230"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Compromised Adform trackpoint-async.js clipper script by SHA256 on endpoint AIDelivery Medium
Retro-hunts the fleet for the exact malicious trojanized Adform tracking library (SHA256 02ff86c7...) landing on disk, typically as a browser cache artifact, to scope which endpoints downloaded the crypto-clipper during the supply-chain window. VirusTotal flagged this file clean across all engines, so hash-based hunting is required rather than AV signal. Rationale: SHA256 02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55 is the pre-extracted hash of the injected library; because VirusTotal shows zero detections, an exact-hash file hunt is the only reliable way to scope endpoint exposure. Cross-checked against: • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e • https://www.it-connect.tech/adform-breach-ad-script-steals-cryptocurrency-for-at-least-a-week/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1115 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A DFIR analyst intentionally saving the sample to an endpoint for analysis
  • A copy of the sample pulled from Beaumont's Pastebin/Archive.org for internal review
  • Malware-repo or IOC-feed clone stored on a workstation
  • SHA256 collision (cryptographically negligible - treat any exact match as true positive)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path (browser cache dir vs a saved copy) and the FileOriginUrl/downloading process to distinguish a real infection from analyst handling. 2) Contain: on genuine infections, clear the affected browser's cache/cookies as Adform advises, block 84.32.102.230, and advise the user to re-check any crypto addresses copied on 26-27 July 2026. 3) Hunt: correlate matching hosts against the C2-beacon UC, and search proxy logs for retrievals of trackpoint-async.js from s2.adform.net/a1.adform.net/ai1.adform.net during the window to build the full impacted-user list.

| where SHA256 == "02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where TargetFileSHA256 == "02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55"

| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Malicious Adform Crypto-Clipper Script Hash on Disk
id: 1a7c9e04-3f28-4d6b-8a52-b9e0c74f1d63
description: Detects the trojanized Adform trackpoint-async.js crypto-clipper library (SHA256 02ff86c7...) written to an endpoint, confirmed clean by all VirusTotal engines and therefore only findable by hash.
references:
  - https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/online-ad-firm-adforms-script-compromised-to-steal-cryptocurrency/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/01
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1115
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Hashes|contains: '02FF86C7F9FE609A753FF15BDA90BAA3C3E0D4A2E559EC4FCF8A3DE0954B7C55'
  condition: selection
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true allow_old_summaries=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_hash="02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false allow_old_summaries=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_hash="02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process Actions on Objectives High
Stealers / wallet drainers read keystore.json, MetaMask, Exodus, Atomic, Phantom data.
ATT&CKT1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Ethereum\keystore\", @"\Bitcoin\", @"\Exodus\", @"\Electrum\wallets\", @"\MetaMask\", @"\Phantom\", @"\Atomic\Local Storage\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Ethereum\keystore\", @"\Bitcoin\",
                                  @"\Exodus\", @"\Electrum\wallets\",
                                  @"\MetaMask\", @"\Phantom\",
                                  @"\Atomic\Local Storage\")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe",

title: Crypto-Wallet Keystore Access by Non-Wallet Process
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d02
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers / wallet drainers read keystore files from MetaMask,
    Exodus, Atomic, Phantom, Bitcoin, Electrum, Ethereum-cli wallets.
    Filtering out the legitimate wallet binaries leaves only attacker
    activity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1005/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1005
    - attack.collection
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Ethereum\keystore\'
            - '\Bitcoin\'
            - '\Exodus\'
            - '\Electrum\wallets\'
            - '\MetaMask\'
            - '\Phantom\'
            - '\Atomic\Local Storage\'
    filter_legit:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\MetaMask.exe'
            - '\Exodus.exe'
            - '\Atomic.exe'
            - '\electrum.exe'
            - '\Bitcoin.exe'
            - '\Phantom.exe'
    condition: selection_path and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
    - Backup software
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("84.32.102.230") or RemoteUrl has_any ("s2.adform.net", "ai1.adform.net", "a1.adform.net")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

let BadDomains = dynamic(["s2.adform.net", "ai1.adform.net", "a1.adform.net"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or SHA1 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or MD5 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or SHA1 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or MD5 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0b
status: experimental

CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard targets travelers worldwide for malware delivery and credential theft

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-31 17 use cases 15 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Storm-2945, a sub-cluster of the Russian threat actor Midnight Blizzard, has been observed compromising the sign-in portals of hospitality-related organizations such as hotels since May 2026 in order to deliver malware to travelers and steal credentials in an operation we call CaptiveCrunch. The post CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard targets travelers worldwide for malware delivery and credential theft appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Captive-portal NCSI hijack: connectivity-check host resolving to Storm-2945 IP · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard targets travelers worldwide for malware deliver
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] CornFlake RAT drop/exec at %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe (Storm-2945) · [LLM] CornFlake 'Cloud Sync Service' (svchost32) service masquerade persistence · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] CaptiveCrunch AiTM/C2 connections to Storm-2945 doppelganger domains and IPs · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Storm-2945 device-code phishing: Entra sign-in / device registration from actor IPs · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
CornFlake RAT drop/exec at %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe (Storm-2945) AIInstallation High
Hunts the CaptiveCrunch CornFlake Go RAT copying itself to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe and executing in dropper mode. Path is a fixed, article-specific artifact — legitimate svchost.exe never runs from per-user AppData. Rationale: Anchored on the exact CornFlake install path named in the Microsoft article body and its own hunting query (Block 3). Real svchost.exe lives only under System32/SysWOW64. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party installer unpacking a helper named svchost32.exe into AppData (rare)
  • Malware-analysis sandbox detonating CornFlake
  • Red-team emulation of Storm-2945
  • Backup tool restoring a quarantined sample
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 and the InitiatingProcess; confirm Go-compiled binary. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill svchost32 tree, quarantine %APPDATA%\svchost32\. 3) Hunt: sweep for the CornFlake service 'Cloud Sync Service', Run keys, scheduled tasks, and beacons to actor domains/IPs; review Entra sign-ins for token theft.
DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where FolderPath endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AccountName, ReportId | order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where EventID == 4688 | where NewProcessName endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe" | project TimeGenerated, Computer, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine, SubjectUserName, Account | order by TimeGenerated desc

CornFlake 'Cloud Sync Service' (svchost32) service masquerade persistence AIInstallation High
Hunts CornFlake persistence via a Windows service named svchost32 with display name 'Cloud Sync Service' and description 'Synchronizes files with the cloud storage provider' — a string tuple unique to the implant. Rationale: Uses the verbatim service name, display name and description strings given in the article — a triple no legitimate Microsoft service uses. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Services Endpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Benign cloud-sync utility named 'Cloud Sync Service' (check ServiceFileName path)
  • GPO/endpoint tooling re-creating a service during remediation testing
  • Red-team persistence emulation
  • Legit backup software installing a sync service (validate signer/path)
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect ImagePath — CornFlake points at %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe not System32. 2) Contain: sc delete svchost32, kill process, isolate host. 3) Hunt: enumerate all four CornFlake persistence mechanisms and check for beacons; expand the service IOC fleet-wide.

CaptiveCrunch AiTM/C2 connections to Storm-2945 doppelganger domains and IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts contact with the CaptiveCrunch actor M365 doppelganger domains (ms365-device.com, ms365-live.com, m365-owa.com, owa-ms365.com) or the six actor IPs used for AitM phishing, malware delivery and C2. Rationale: Uses the four doppelganger domains and six IPs published by Microsoft and cross-confirmed by ReliaQuest (ms365-live.com cited by both for device-code phishing). Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/
ATT&CKT1557 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst/sandbox browsing the doppelganger domain during investigation
  • EASM scanner probing actor IPs
  • Passive-DNS/blocklist sync pre-resolving IOC domains
  • Actor IP later reassigned to a benign tenant (check campaign window)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess — browser = AitM landing, svchost32/AppData binary = active C2. 2) Contain: block domains/IPs, isolate host, revoke Entra sessions. 3) Hunt: pull Entra sign-in/device-registration logs, check CornFlake install path/service, review peers on the same captive-portal segment.

Storm-2945 device-code phishing: Entra sign-in / device registration from actor IPs AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts successful Entra sign-ins and device registrations from the six CaptiveCrunch actor IPs — the credential/token-theft stage where Storm-2945 abuses the device code auth flow (Microsoft Authentication Broker) to register attacker devices and mint PRTs. Rationale: Pivots successful Entra sign-ins on the six actor IPs; ReliaQuest and the Storm-2372 report both confirm device-code flow abuse (ms365-live.com) leading to OAuth token theft and device registration. Falcon left empty — Azure sign-in telemetry is not in FDR. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/
ATT&CKT1528 T1621 T1098.005
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • VPN/NAT egress sharing an IP later reassigned to actor space (check campaign window)
  • TI platform doing authenticated IOC validation from a lab tenant
  • Traveler via proxy reusing hosting IP space (confirm via device compliance)
  • Pentest emulating device-code phishing
Suppression filter
| where AppDisplayName has_any ("Microsoft Authentication Broker", "Device Registration") or ClientAppUsed == "Mobile Apps and Desktop clients"
Response runbook
1) Triage: review AppDisplayName/ResourceDisplayName (Microsoft Authentication Broker + Device Registration Service is the signature) and whether a new device registered immediately after. 2) Contain: revoke refresh tokens/sessions, disable/re-enroll account, remove attacker-registered devices, block IPs in CA. 3) Hunt: enumerate device registrations and OAuth consents, check Graph mail exfiltration, correlate with captive-portal usage and endpoint CornFlake IOCs.

Captive-portal NCSI hijack: connectivity-check host resolving to Storm-2945 IP AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the CaptiveCrunch initial-access primitive — DNS/HTTP manipulation of OS/browser connectivity-check (NCSI) endpoints so they resolve to actor IPs, which is how Storm-2945 injects the fake browser/OS-update ClickFix landing. Rationale: Combines the NCSI endpoint list from the article's own hunting query (Block 1) with the six actor IPs — a known connectivity host answering to a Storm-2945 IP fingerprints the captive-portal DNS/HTTP manipulation that seeds ClickFix delivery. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/
ATT&CKT1557 T1584.002 T1204.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Corporate transparent proxy/CDN rewriting NCSI answers (validate IP is an actor IP)
  • DNS sinkhole intentionally redirecting connectivity checks
  • Split-horizon DNS returning private answers
  • Passive-DNS collector replaying historical records
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the resolved IP is one of the six actor IPs and which SSID the device used — hospitality/conference Wi-Fi is expected. 2) Contain: get the user off the hostile network (full-tunnel VPN), block IPs, inspect for a fake-update executable download and CornFlake install path. 3) Hunt: correlate to ClickFix execution, CornFlake persistence, and device-code sign-ins from the actor IPs for the same user.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

NocoBase CVE-2026-52887 SQLi in /api/myInAppChannels:list filter param AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the NocoBase in-app-message channel listing endpoint whose latestMsgReceiveTimestamp $lt filter carries SQL rather than an epoch integer. Legit clients send a numeric timestamp; any SQL keyword (pg_sleep, union, copy, program) in that parameter is a direct exploit attempt for the Sequelize.literal() injection. Rationale: Endpoint path myInAppChannels:list plus the exact vulnerable filter field latestMsgReceiveTimestamp are unique to this CVE; a legit $lt is a plain epoch integer, so any SQL token co-occurring is near-zero-FP exploit evidence. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p849-8hwh-84j9 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@nocobase/plugin-collection-sql/CVE-2026-52888/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-41641/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized DAST/WAF scanner (Burp, sqlmap, Acunetix) sweeping the app in a sanctioned pentest
  • Vulnerability-management tooling replaying the public PoC against an internal test instance
  • Security researcher validating the patch on a staging host
  • WAF logging a request it already blocked (check status/DeviceAction to confirm delivery)
Suppression filter
| where not (HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("sqlmap","nuclei","acunetix") and SrcIpAddr in ("10.0.0.0/8"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request from proxy logs — confirm the $lt value contains SQL (pg_sleep/union/copy) and note SrcIpAddr, User-Agent, and HTTP status (200 = likely reached the handler). Check whether the same IP hit /api/auth:signUp/signIn first. 2) Contain: block SrcIpAddr at the WAF/edge, disable the anonymous auth-basic signUp (allowSignUp:false), and upgrade @nocobase/plugin-notification-in-app-message to 2.0.61+. 3) Hunt: look for postgres spawning shells (UC2) on the DB host and for COPY TO PROGRAM / SELECT ... FROM users artefacts; rotate the super-admin password (PBKDF2 hash may be exfiltrated).
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "myInAppChannels" and Url has "latestMsgReceiveTimestamp"
| where Url has_any ("pg_sleep","sleep(","union","select","program","copy","--","case when")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, Url, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PostgreSQL COPY TO PROGRAM shell spawn (postgres → sh) — NocoBase RCE AIInstallation High
Detects the RCE tail of CVE-2026-52887 where a stacked COPY ... TO PROGRAM statement makes the postgres backend fork a shell as uid=999(postgres) inside the DB container. The postgres daemon spawning sh/bash/id/curl is anomalous and high-fidelity regardless of the web-tier signal. Rationale: The article verifies COPY ... TO PROGRAM runs shell as uid=999(postgres); a postgres parent spawning sh/id/curl is a behaviour the DB daemon never exhibits in normal operation, making the parent→child pair itself the detection. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p849-8hwh-84j9 • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-41641/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • archive_command / restore_command config invoking a shell for WAL archiving
  • PostgreSQL extensions (pg_cron, plsh, pg_backrest wrappers) legitimately shelling out
  • DBA-run maintenance script executed under the postgres service account
  • Container entrypoint/health-check scripts parented to the postgres PID tree
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("archive_command","restore_command","pg_basebackup","pgbackrest","barman"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child ProcessCommandLine — a COPY TO PROGRAM payload typically shows sh -c '<attacker cmd>' (id, curl to external IP, reverse shell). Confirm the parent is the real postgres backend and not a wrapper. 2) Contain: isolate the DB container/host, kill the child process tree, and revoke the nocobase role's superuser (ALTER ROLE nocobase NOSUPERUSER); patch to 2.0.61+. 3) Hunt: review postgres logs for COPY/CREATE statements, check /tmp for dropped files (e.g. PWN_VERIFY.txt), enumerate outbound connections from the DB host, and rotate any credentials readable from the DB (users.password hashes).

| order by Timestamp desc

| order by TimeGenerated desc
