NocoBase anonymous auth:signUp followed by myInAppChannels exploit from same IP AIDelivery Medium
Correlates the anonymous account-creation step (POST /api/auth:signUp?authenticator=basic, enabled by default) with a subsequent SQLi request to myInAppChannels:list from the same source IP inside a short window. Captures the full anonymous-reach chain the advisory describes: sign up, sign in, inject. Rationale: Ties the advisory's exact anonymous-reach primitives — /api/auth:signUp?authenticator=basic and the myInAppChannels SQLi — into one same-IP chain, which is far higher fidelity than either request alone and evidences intent, not just scanning. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p849-8hwh-84j9
ATT&CKT1136 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate new user self-registering then normally browsing in-app notifications (no SQL tokens — filtered out)
  • QA/automation account provisioning that also exercises the notifications API
  • Shared corporate egress IP where an unrelated real signup and a scanner hit within the window
  • Load-testing harness creating accounts and querying channels
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the exploit request from the correlated IP actually carries SQL in latestMsgReceiveTimestamp and returned 200; identify the newly created username via the signUp request body/response. 2) Contain: disable/delete the attacker-created account, block the SrcIpAddr, set auth-basic allowSignUp:false, and upgrade to 2.0.61+. 3) Hunt: enumerate all accounts created from that IP/subnet, review whether the account reached other loggedIn ACL resources, and pivot to UC2 to check for postgres shell execution on the DB tier.
let Window = 1h;
let SignUps = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Url has "auth:signUp"
    | project SignupTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "myInAppChannels" and Url has "latestMsgReceiveTimestamp"
| where Url has_any ("pg_sleep","union","select","program","sleep","copy","--")
| join kind=inner SignUps on SrcIpAddr
| where TimeGenerated between (SignupTime .. SignupTime + Window)
| project SignupTime, ExploitTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, Url, HttpStatusCode, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by ExploitTime desc

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.process_name,
       Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Suspected Chinese-Speaking Hackers Target Central Asian Governments With OctLurk

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OctLurk/SilkLurk/LurkProxy C2 beacon to campaign domains & IPs · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Impacket secretsdump DC hash harvesting via OctLurk shell plugin · [LLM] Fscan internal/public scanning with pp.txt credential file · [LLM] SilkLurk share collection & WinRAR/7-Zip staging via cmd/PowerShell · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
OctLurk/SilkLurk/LurkProxy C2 beacon to campaign domains & IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts host-to-C2 traffic to the hard-coded OctLurk/SilkLurk/LurkProxy infrastructure named by Kaspersky (connectivity-check domain dns.ssentialserv.xyz, OctLurk C2 dns.multitoconference.com, LurkProxy C2 154.196.162.76, plus the campaign's dynamic-DNS and IP set). Article-specific because it keys on the exact indicator bundle rather than generic beaconing. Rationale: Uses the exact IOC bundle (connectivity-check dns.ssentialserv.xyz, OctLurk C2 dns.multitoconference.com, LurkProxy C2 154.196.162.76) cross-checked against Securelist and gbhackers write-ups; dynamic-DNS domains (gleeze.com/kozow.com/casacam.net) are article-specific hostnames. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1095
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox detonation host resolving the same IOCs during analysis
  • Security researcher pivoting on the domains from a corporate endpoint
  • Passive DNS/monitoring appliance pre-resolving indicator feeds
  • Recycled dynamic-DNS hostname (gleeze/kozow) later re-registered by a benign party
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which internal host resolved/connected and identify the initiating process (InitiatingProcessFileName) — a loader/rundll32/unsigned binary is high-confidence malicious. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the domain/IP at DNS+firewall, and snapshot memory (both families are memory-resident). 3) Hunt: on the same host look for the LurkProxy batch launcher, Impacket secretsdump, fscan+pp.txt, and AnyDesk-masquerading keylogger from the other UCs; sweep the org for any other host touching the IOC list.

Impacket secretsdump DC hash harvesting via OctLurk shell plugin AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts execution of Impacket's secretsdump.py used by the OctLurk command-shell plugin to dump password hashes from domain controllers. Article-specific because it keys on the named tool string and the DCSync/NTDS dumping flags. Rationale: Keys on the article-named tool 'secretsdump.py' plus its DCSync/NTDS dumping flags — corroborated by Securelist describing DC hash harvesting; machine-account exclusion keeps it tight. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1003.006 T1003.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized red-team / penetration test using Impacket
  • IR team collecting NTDS during a DFIR engagement
  • Security tooling QA that ships Impacket in a test harness
  • Named file coincidentally containing 'secretsdump' string in an unrelated script repo checkout
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\\pentest\\" and AccountName !in~ ("redteam","pentester")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is a DC or a host with domain-admin context; capture the full command line and parent process (loader vs python). 2) Contain: isolate the host, force-reset krbtgt twice and any exposed privileged accounts, invalidate cached hashes. 3) Hunt: pivot on the initiating account across DCs, look for prior OctLurk C2 (UC1), lateral movement to file shares (UC5), and fscan/pp.txt spraying (UC3).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "secretsdump" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-just-dc", "-just-dc-ntlm", "-outputfile") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ntds", "lsa", "sam")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "secretsdump" or (CommandLine has_any ("-just-dc", "-just-dc-ntlm") and CommandLine has_any ("ntds","lsa","sam"))
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fscan internal/public scanning with pp.txt credential file AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the campaign's use of Fscan to scan for SSH (22) and MySQL (3306) and to spray credentials from a password file named pp.txt. Article-specific via the exact 'pp.txt' filename and fscan port targets rather than generic port scanning. Rationale: Uses the exact 'pp.txt' password-file name and the fscan SSH-22/MySQL-3306 target profile stated in the article — corroborated by Securelist's description of the scanning stage; both are specific enough to be low-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1046 T1110.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scan / red-team recon using fscan
  • Sysadmin ad-hoc port check that happens to include 22 and 3306
  • A benign file legitimately named pp.txt passed to an unrelated tool
  • Security researcher running fscan in a lab segment
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has @"\\Tools\\Scanners\\" and AccountName !in~ ("vulnscan-svc")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line to see scanned CIDR ranges and confirm pp.txt existence/contents on the host. 2) Contain: isolate the scanning host, rotate any credentials present in pp.txt, and block SSH/MySQL from that source internally. 3) Hunt: correlate scanned hosts with subsequent successful logons, and check the same host for OctLurk C2 (UC1) and secretsdump (UC2).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "fscan" or FileName startswith "fscan" or ProcessCommandLine has "pp.txt" or (ProcessCommandLine has_all ("-p","22","3306") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-h","-pwdf","-rf"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "fscan" or CommandLine has "pp.txt" or (CommandLine has_all ("-p","22","3306") and CommandLine has_any ("-pwdf","-rf"))
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Keylogger masquerading as AnyDesk (name/path/publisher mismatch) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the campaign's keylogger that masquerades as AnyDesk to evade detection, by flagging anydesk.exe processes whose signer/company or install path does not match the legitimate AnyDesk product. Article-specific because masquerading-as-AnyDesk is the named evasion trick. Rationale: The article explicitly states the keylogger 'masquerades as AnyDesk to sidestep detection' — flagging anydesk.exe with a publisher/path mismatch is the direct behavioural pivot on that named trick. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1056.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portable/custom AnyDesk deployed via MSP tooling to a non-standard folder
  • AnyDesk run from Downloads/Temp by an end user before install
  • Software-packaging/SCCM staging AnyDesk in a temp cache path
  • AnyDesk MSI extracted to a custom enterprise directory
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ccmexec.exe","msiexec.exe","setup.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the binary's signer and hash against known-good AnyDesk; an unsigned or mismatched-company anydesk.exe is high-confidence malicious. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and preserve the on-disk sample for the keylog-output file. 3) Hunt: look for keystroke-capture output files, browser-credential theft, and OctLurk C2 (UC1) on the same host; sweep for the same SHA256 org-wide.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "anydesk.exe"
| where ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName != "AnyDesk Software GmbH"
    or (FolderPath !has @"\\Program Files\\AnyDesk" and FolderPath !has @"\\Program Files (x86)\\AnyDesk" and FolderPath !has @"\\AppData\\Roaming\\AnyDesk")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has "anydesk.exe"
| where NewProcessName !has @"\\Program Files\\AnyDesk" and NewProcessName !has @"\\Program Files (x86)\\AnyDesk" and NewProcessName !has @"\\AppData\\Roaming\\AnyDesk"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SilkLurk share collection & WinRAR/7-Zip staging via cmd/PowerShell AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the SilkLurk post-compromise chain where cmd.exe launches PowerShell to mount admin shares, stage confidential documents, and archive them with WinRAR/7-Zip for exfil. Article-specific via the parent (cmd/PowerShell) plus legitimate-archiver staging behaviour tied to net-share access. Rationale: Maps to the article's SilkLurk description of cmd.exe launching PowerShell to reach admin shares and using WinRAR/7-Zip to archive stolen data; the archiver-under-cmd/PowerShell parent plus archive flags is the article-specific collection pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1560.001 T1039
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin/backup script archiving logs or profiles via 7-Zip from a batch file
  • Software-build pipeline invoking rar/7z from cmd for packaging
  • Helpdesk collecting user data into an archive over a share
  • Legitimate scheduled task compressing a network folder for backup
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "Backup" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "scheduledtask"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the archive path/name and source (net use to admin shares beforehand?); confidential-doc paths + password-protected (-hp) archives are high-confidence. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the staged archive before exfil, and revoke the admin credentials used for the share mount. 3) Hunt: check for prior SilkLurk DLL side-loading / PlugX, subsequent egress to the C2 IOC set (UC1), and other hosts staging the same archive naming pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("rar.exe","winrar.exe","7z.exe","7za.exe","7zg.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (" a ", "-hp", "-p", "-r ", " a -")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\rar.exe","\\winrar.exe","\\7z.exe","\\7za.exe","\\7zg.exe")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any (" a ","-hp"," a -","-r ")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Archiver Spawned by cmd/PowerShell for Data Staging (SilkLurk)
id: a3f2c8b1-7e94-4d05-9c26-5b1a0e7f4d38
description: WinRAR/7-Zip archiving spawned from cmd.exe or PowerShell to stage confidential documents, as seen in the SilkLurk post-compromise chain
references:
  - https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/31
tags:
  - attack.collection
  - attack.t1560.001
  - attack.t1039
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\rar.exe'
      - '\winrar.exe'
      - '\7z.exe'
      - '\7za.exe'
      - '\7zg.exe'
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - ' a '
      - '-hp'
      - '-r '
  filter_machine:
    User|endswith: '$'
  condition: selection and not filter_machine
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\cmd.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\CMD.EXE OR *\PowerShell.exe) @Image:(*\rar.exe OR *\winrar.exe OR *\7z.exe OR *\7za.exe OR *\WinRAR.exe OR *\7z.EXE) @CommandLine:(*\ a\ * OR *-hp* OR *-r\ *)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\(rar|winrar|7z|7za|7zg)\.exe$/i
| ParentBaseFileName=/(cmd|powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| regex("(\\s+a\\s+|-hp|-r\\s+)", field=CommandLine)
| NOT UserName=/\$$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("rar.exe","winrar.exe","7z.exe","7za.exe","7zg.exe")) AND (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")) AND (Processes.process="*a *" OR Processes.process="* a *" OR Processes.process="*-hp*" OR Processes.process="*-r *") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("rar.exe","winrar.exe","7z.exe","7za.exe","7zg.exe")) AND (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")) AND (Processes.process="*a *" OR Processes.process="* a *" OR Processes.process="*-hp*" OR Processes.process="*-r *") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental

references:

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"

        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.

        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("082d49ef9f14e6811d68c7e0e82e5069", "f4578e869a735cfad691f927bae3e638", "7c2f64461bb519c6cbf1fc687675514c", "8269d6ba1b6842f9152c90cf7add9b93", "a0cc7accc79abb0287aaba825d0351f0", "a56cce62930a6bee80d679b4c495a340", "1415a78b75de7db4ba3d1e61d7db4501", "a4d550a3ba0cd073fe3839b99d98a7a8", "2a571f6cee42a17d873f4c942649813f", "37dc84e4bcad92fa28f1e7778d088283", "cf903e4a1629aa0582fd0363b5786676", "3c9a1ba8e0c7475706adc6376e9d7b7c", "ef59aad625eebda8650aec5820d6ce69", "32a5985543433a4f60da2fafd873b927", "18dc8bff47cc282508354771d0c8cf8c", "9a1dd1d96481d61934dcc2d568971d06") or SHA1 in~ ("082d49ef9f14e6811d68c7e0e82e5069", "f4578e869a735cfad691f927bae3e638", "7c2f64461bb519c6cbf1fc687675514c", "8269d6ba1b6842f9152c90cf7add9b93", "a0cc7accc79abb0287aaba825d0351f0", "a56cce62930a6bee80d679b4c495a340", "1415a78b75de7db4ba3d1e61d7db4501", "a4d550a3ba0cd073fe3839b99d98a7a8", "2a571f6cee42a17d873f4c942649813f", "37dc84e4bcad92fa28f1e7778d088283", "cf903e4a1629aa0582fd0363b5786676", "3c9a1ba8e0c7475706adc6376e9d7b7c", "ef59aad625eebda8650aec5820d6ce69", "32a5985543433a4f60da2fafd873b927", "18dc8bff47cc282508354771d0c8cf8c", "9a1dd1d96481d61934dcc2d568971d06") or MD5 in~ ("082d49ef9f14e6811d68c7e0e82e5069", "f4578e869a735cfad691f927bae3e638", "7c2f64461bb519c6cbf1fc687675514c", "8269d6ba1b6842f9152c90cf7add9b93", "a0cc7accc79abb0287aaba825d0351f0", "a56cce62930a6bee80d679b4c495a340", "1415a78b75de7db4ba3d1e61d7db4501", "a4d550a3ba0cd073fe3839b99d98a7a8", "2a571f6cee42a17d873f4c942649813f", "37dc84e4bcad92fa28f1e7778d088283", "cf903e4a1629aa0582fd0363b5786676", "3c9a1ba8e0c7475706adc6376e9d7b7c", "ef59aad625eebda8650aec5820d6ce69", "32a5985543433a4f60da2fafd873b927", "18dc8bff47cc282508354771d0c8cf8c", "9a1dd1d96481d61934dcc2d568971d06")

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

CVE-2026-3055 NetScaler SAML IdP memory-overread scrape (rapid /saml/login loop) AIExploitation High
Hunts the memory-disclosure exploitation Unit 42 confirmed against Citrix NetScaler: a source IP hammering the SAML IdP /saml/login endpoint in a tight loop to repeatedly overread heap memory and harvest session cookies. Normal SAML SSO produces a handful of /saml/login hits per user; 50+ from one IP in 10 minutes is a memory-scrape loop. Rationale: Grounds on the corroborated CVE-2026-3055 exploit path: unauthenticated crafted SAMLRequest to /saml/login (AssertionConsumerServiceURL omitted) leaking heap via NSC_TASS. The loop-volume threshold captures the repeated-overread behaviour needed to reassemble cookies. defender_kql/datadog/falcon empty: a NetScaler appliance is not onboarded to Defender XDR/FDR and inbound appliance web logs have no clean Datadog source; the detection lives in CEF (Sentinel) and the CIM Web datamodel (Splunk). Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/vulnerabilities/cve-2026-3055/ • https://socradar.io/blog/cve-2026-3055-netscaler-memory-disclosure/ • https://github.com/rapid7/metasploit-framework/pull/21204 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chinese-hacker-commands-deepseek-via.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1212
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scan (Nessus/Qualys/Nuclei) hitting the SAML endpoint in bulk
  • Corporate egress NAT concentrating many real SSO users behind one public IP during a morning login storm
  • SSO gateway / load-balancer health probes polling /saml/login
  • SAML federation partner proxy relaying many users' auth from a single IP
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Nuclei","masscan","zgrab","Expanse")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SourceIP's full /saml/login request stream — confirm the requests carry SAMLRequest bodies missing AssertionConsumerServiceURL and check NetScaler version against the CVE-2026-3055 patched build; look for abnormally large responses. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the ADC/WAF, and if the appliance is unpatched and SAML-IdP-configured, take it out of rotation and rotate all AAA/LDAP bind credentials and session secrets that could have been in memory. 3) Hunt: enumerate every NSC_AAAC/NSC_TASS session active after the scrape window and pivot to UC2 (cookie reuse) to find hijacked sessions; review authentication logs for the leaked accounts.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DeviceVendor has "Citrix" or DeviceProduct has_any ("NetScaler","ADC","Gateway")
| where RequestURL has "/saml/login"
| summarize RequestCount = count(),
            SampleUrl = any(RequestURL),
            Appliances = make_set(DestinationHostName, 5),
            UserAgents = make_set(RequestClientApplication, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where RequestCount > 50   // 50+ /saml/login hits in 10m from one IP = CVE-2026-3055 memory-scrape loop, not normal SAML SSO
| order by RequestCount desc

Network communication with Iranian-APT infrastructure targeting Rockwell PLCs (185.82.73.160-171 / 135.136.1.133) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts any inbound or outbound network flow to the ULTAHOST operator workstation range (185.82.73.160-171, AS214036) or the M247 staging box (135.136.1.133, AS9009) tied by CISA/Censys to the coordinated attacks on U.S. water-sector PLCs. High-fidelity because these are dedicated single-purpose attacker hosts, not shared services. Rationale: Uses the exact attacker IPs from the article's IOC block, refined against the Censys bundle (12 IPs across the ULTAHOST /28 operator range plus the M247 single-use staging box). Dedicated attacker infrastructure = near-zero-FP alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://censys.com/blog/iranian-affiliated-apt-targeting-rockwell-allen-bradley-plcs/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/07/30/cisa-urges-water-and-wastewater-systems-sector-protect-ot-against-activity-targeting-plcs • https://www.fbi.gov/news/press-releases/malicious-cyber-actors-targeting-water-and-wastewater-sector-internet--facing-programmable-logic-controllers-causing-operational-disruptions
ATT&CKT0883 T0886 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internet-wide scanners or threat-intel crawlers (Shodan/Censys/Shadowserver) that happen to be re-homed onto the same ULTAHOST /28 after attacker teardown
  • A security researcher or your own red team pivoting through a rented ULTAHOST/M247 VPS in the same range
  • Threat-intel platform (e.g. MISP/VT) sandbox detonations reaching out to the IPs from an analyst subnet
  • Legitimate SaaS re-provisioned onto a recycled ULTAHOST IP months later (infra churn)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal asset (DeviceName/SourceIP) and whether the flow is inbound (attempted access to an exposed PLC/HMI/engineering box) or outbound (possible beacon); pull the port — 44818/2222/43589 or RDP raise severity. 2) Contain: block the IP set at the perimeter and OT DMZ firewall in both directions, isolate the internal host, and pull the affected PLC's known-good image offline per Rockwell's MicroLogix 1400 recovery notice in case credentials were changed. 3) Hunt: sweep 30d of firewall/EDR for any of the 12 IPs, for inbound EtherNet/IP on TCP 44818 to OT subnets, and for unexpected RDP to non-standard ports; validate no PLC IP/password changes occurred.

Surfaces the exact exposure CISA warns about: internet-reachable Rockwell/Allen-Bradley PLCs (and HMIs) accepting EtherNet/IP (TCP 44818) or TCP 2222 connections directly from public source addresses — the vector the Iranian-affiliated actors used to reach MicroLogix 1400 / CompactLogix / Micro850 controllers and change their IPs and passwords. Durable even after attacker IPs rotate. Rationale: Pivots on EtherNet/IP TCP 44818 (plus the TCP 2222 secondary target) confirmed by the Censys write-up as the protocol/ports the actors used against exposed Rockwell controllers; scoping to public source IPs isolates the internet-exposure condition CISA/FBI told operators to eliminate. Firewall CEF is the primary source since PLCs don't run EDR; Defender clause covers Rockwell engineering/HMI Windows hosts that also listen on 44818. Cross-checked against: • https://censys.com/blog/iranian-affiliated-apt-targeting-rockwell-allen-bradley-plcs/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/07/30/cisa-urges-water-and-wastewater-systems-sector-protect-ot-against-activity-targeting-plcs • https://www.securityweek.com/cisa-urges-water-sector-to-protect-ot-after-coordinated-attacks-on-plcs/
ATT&CKT0883 T0819 T0886
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized remote SCADA integrator/vendor connecting over a public IP because a site-to-site VPN was down or misconfigured
  • Internet background-noise scanners (Shodan, Censys, Shadowserver, academic scanners) probing TCP 44818
  • Carrier-grade NAT / cellular-modem egress making a legitimately-internal engineering host appear to have a public peer
  • Scheduled penetration test or attack-surface-management scan against the OT DMZ
  • A cloud-hosted historian/telemetry gateway legitimately polling PLCs over EtherNet/IP across a public link
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("198.20.69.0/24","198.20.70.0/24","66.240.192.0/18","71.6.128.0/17","185.163.109.0/24") // exclude Shodan/Censys/Shadowserver research scanner ranges
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the DestinationIP is an OT asset (PLC/HMI/engineering station) and whether the SourceIP is a known integrator/scanner; any public source touching 44818 on a controller is treated as exposure until proven otherwise. 2) Contain: remove the asset from direct internet exposure (front it with VPN/gateway per CISA), apply an IP allow-list on the firewall, and change default/known passwords; verify the PLC image against a known-good backup. 3) Hunt: enumerate every OT asset with inbound 44818/2222/VNC(5900)/Telnet(23) from public space, cross-check those SourceIPs against the 185.82.73.160-171 and 135.136.1.133 IOCs, and review PLC config-change/loss-of-comms events around first-seen.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort in (44818, 2222)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationPort in (44818, 2222)
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count(), SrcIPs=make_set(SourceIP, 50) by DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by Hits desc

HollowFrame Loader Deploys Matryoshka Backdoor in Spear-Phishing Attack on Law Firm

The Hacker News
2026-07-31 17 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have shed light on a previously undocumented Go-based loader framework called HollowFrame and a Rust-based malware family tracked as Matryoshka. According to Blackpoint Cyber, the intrusion sequence begins with a spear-phishing message containing a link to an encrypted archive, which holds a Windows Shortcut (LNK). Executing the file triggers a multi-stage chain that

HollowFrame LNK delivery: cmd.exe writes payload, certutil -decode to .cmd, PowerShell fetch AIDelivery High
Hunts the HollowFrame 'Case Documents' LNK execution chain in which explorer-spawned cmd.exe writes a payload, certutil.exe decodes it to a .cmd, and a second cmd.exe /K launches PowerShell to pull next-stage code. Anchored on the certutil -decode-to-.cmd step, which is rare in benign use and is the pivot shown in Blackpoint's process-tree diagram. Rationale: Uses the exact certutil -decode-to-.cmd step and explorer/cmd parentage from the article's process-tree image (cmd.png); certutil writing a .cmd under an interactive shell is high-fidelity and near-never benign. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hollowframe-loader-deploys-matryoshka.html • https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/paperwork-to-payload-from-shortcut-clicks-to-rundll32-execution/ • https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhEQz5wx5Wk3F3uCiiNzfwmlWu3vgQN2TohgoaIdhGjyVcu05SfUmZjzmClUPOkK9M6-S06GZJ4jDqesb_2AYetLTuebp9_K8-Dkfp88cjAJYrzNhyPBwTJ_CD1gWAGuo0cnEz7Mx8eb1r0A5_gv6xsACyEPByhr-COEjfyVn1lIBEJNHK44Vfk7EHCtmHK/s1700-e365/cmd.png
ATT&CKT1140 T1059.001 T1204.002 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit software installers using certutil to decode embedded config into a .cmd (rare)
  • Admin scripts that base64-encode/decode batch files for transport
  • Security-tooling deployment scripts that stage .cmd via certutil
  • CI/build agents invoking certutil under cmd.exe
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("MpCmdRun","ccmsetup","choco") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the host — confirm explorer.exe→cmd.exe /c→certutil→cmd.exe /K→powershell.exe and inspect the decoded .cmd content and the PowerShell command line for the staging IP 2.26.252.84. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, kill the powershell/cmd chain, and capture the dropped .cmd and any files written to Temp/Public. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same user's mailbox for the 'Case Documents' lure and check other hosts for certutil -decode + outbound to 2.26.252.84 / 45.158.196.184.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "certutil.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "decode"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".cmd"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","explorer.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\certutil.exe"
| where CommandLine has "decode" and CommandLine has ".cmd"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\explorer.exe"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: HollowFrame certutil Decode of Payload to CMD Script
id: 6f2c1a44-7e0b-4d3a-9a6c-2b91e5d8c401
description: Detects certutil.exe decoding a base64 payload into a .cmd file spawned from cmd.exe/explorer.exe, the HollowFrame LNK delivery step.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hollowframe-loader-deploys-matryoshka.html
  - https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/paperwork-to-payload-from-shortcut-clicks-to-rundll32-execution/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/31
tags:

logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\certutil.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'decode'
      - '.cmd'
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\explorer.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\certutil.exe OR *\CertUtil.exe OR *\CERTUTIL.EXE) @CommandLine:(*decode*) @CommandLine:(*.cmd*) @ParentImage:(*\cmd.exe OR *\CMD.EXE OR *\explorer.exe OR *\EXPLORER.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\certutil\.exe$/i
| regex("decode", field=CommandLine)
| regex("\.cmd", field=CommandLine)
| ParentBaseFileName=/(cmd|explorer)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=certutil.exe (Processes.process="*-decode*" OR Processes.process="*/decode*") Processes.process="*.cmd*" (Processes.parent_process_name=cmd.exe OR Processes.parent_process_name=explorer.exe) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
HollowFrame staging server download (PowerShell fetch from 2.26.252.84) AIDelivery Medium
Alerts on any endpoint egress to the HollowFrame next-stage staging host 2.26.252.84, or a PowerShell command line referencing that IP. This is the payload-retrieval step after the LNK/certutil chain and uses a hardcoded article IOC. Rationale: 2.26.252.84 is the article's explicitly named PowerShell fetch/staging IP; direct IOC match on any endpoint egress is high-fidelity delivery evidence. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hollowframe-loader-deploys-matryoshka.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic

  • Security researcher lab traffic
  • Proxy/EDR appliance re-checking the indicator
  • Shared NAT gateway where another benign host reused the IP after takedown
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection — expect powershell.exe/cmd.exe descended from explorer→certutil chain; confirm on-host payload artifacts. 2) Contain: block 2.26.252.84 at the egress firewall/proxy and isolate any endpoint that connected. 3) Hunt: sweep for the certutil -decode chain (UC1) and any subsequent connections to 45.158.196.184:8888 and github.com/adioziaete/memio.

| order by Timestamp desc

| where DstIpAddr == "2.26.252.84"

HollowFrame DLL side-load: python.exe loading rogue python311.dll from user-writable path AIInstallation High
Hunts the HollowFrame loader's signed-binary side-load pair — legitimate python.exe loading a malicious python311.dll from a non-standard, user-writable directory (Temp, Public, AppData\Roaming, ProgramData) rather than a real Python install root. Rationale: Uses the article's exact side-load pair python.exe + python311.dll and constrains to user-writable directories to separate the HollowFrame drop from real Python installs; corroborated by a public Joe Sandbox python311.dll analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hollowframe-loader-deploys-matryoshka.html • https://www.joesandbox.com/analysis/1651022/2/html
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1055
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portable/embedded Python bundles shipped inside app folders under ProgramData
  • Developer venv or PyInstaller onedir builds unpacked to Temp
  • Data-science tooling running python from a Downloads folder
  • Vendor agents embedding a private Python runtime outside Program Files
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Anaconda3\", @"\miniconda3\", @"\venv\", @"\.venv\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash python311.dll and check reputation/signing; a Rust/Go-linked or unsigned python311.dll next to python.exe in Temp is malicious. 2) Contain: isolate host, quarantine the DLL + python.exe copy, and kill the process tree. 3) Hunt: look for the follow-on side-load (version.dll/wtsapi32.dll), scheduled-task persistence, and C2 to 45.158.196.184:8888 or GitHub adioziaete/memio.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "python.exe"

Matryoshka side-load: version.dll / wtsapi32.dll loaded from outside System32 AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Matryoshka backdoor's side-loaded proxy DLLs — version.dll and wtsapi32.dll — being loaded from any directory outside C:\Windows\System32/SysWOW64/WinSxS. These are genuine Windows library names abused via search-order hijack to run the Rust backdoor. Rationale: version.dll and wtsapi32.dll are the exact Matryoshka side-load DLL names in the article; constraining to loads outside Windows system directories isolates search-order hijack from legitimate OS use. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hollowframe-loader-deploys-matryoshka.html
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit third-party apps that ship their own version.dll/wtsapi32.dll in their install directory (common for games/media apps)
  • Portable applications run from USB/Downloads
  • Software installers staging DLLs in Temp before moving to Program Files
  • Developer build outputs containing copied system DLLs
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Downloads\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the DLL's signer and the host process — an unsigned version.dll/wtsapi32.dll in Temp/AppData loaded by a non-OS binary is the Matryoshka indicator; hash and detonate. 2) Contain: isolate the host and quarantine the DLL + its loader. 3) Hunt: correlate with the python311.dll side-load (UC3), scheduled-task persistence, and outbound to 45.158.196.184:8888 or api.github.com for adioziaete/memio.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("version.dll","wtsapi32.dll")
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\Windows\System32\", @"\Windows\SysWOW64\", @"\Windows\WinSxS\"))
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("version.dll","wtsapi32.dll")
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\Windows\System32\", @"\Windows\SysWOW64\", @"\Windows\WinSxS\"))
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Matryoshka HTTP C2 beacon to 45.158.196.184:8888 AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on endpoint egress to the Matryoshka backdoor's hardcoded HTTP C2 endpoint 45.158.196.184 on TCP 8888, used by the version.dll variant to spawn a shell and deliver tooling. Uses a fixed IP+port article IOC. Rationale: 45.158.196.184:8888 is the article's explicit Matryoshka HTTP C2 endpoint; a fixed IP+non-standard-port pair is high-confidence C2 evidence with negligible benign traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hollowframe-loader-deploys-matryoshka.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandbox/lab detonation of the sample
  • Threat-intel appliance validating the IOC
  • Reuse of the IP by a benign service post-takedown
  • Internal proxy re-checking indicator reputation
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess connecting to 45.158.196.184:8888 — expect a version.dll-hosting signed binary or python.exe; capture the process tree back to the LNK chain. 2) Contain: block the IP at egress, isolate the host, and terminate the beaconing process. 3) Hunt: enumerate AD reconnaissance activity (net/nltest/ldap), scheduled-task persistence, and GitHub C2 to adioziaete/memio on the same and adjacent hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "45.158.196.184" and RemotePort == 8888
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "45.158.196.184" and DstPortNumber == 8888
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Matryoshka GitHub C2: non-browser process polling api.github.com / raw.githubusercontent.com AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the Matryoshka wtsapi32.dll variant that uses a private GitHub repo (adioziaete/memio) as C2 — beacon.json/cmd.json/result.json per-host mailboxes. Since traffic is HTTPS, this surfaces unexpected, non-developer processes (python.exe, rundll32, or side-loaded DLL hosts) reaching GitHub API/raw endpoints. Rationale: Article names the private GitHub repo adioziaete/memio and the beacon.json/cmd.json/result.json mailbox structure as C2; HTTPS hides the path, so the detectable pivot is unusual non-dev processes reaching GitHub API/raw hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hollowframe-loader-deploys-matryoshka.html
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Package managers (pip, npm, go) pulling from raw.githubusercontent.com
  • Update frameworks/agents fetching release assets from GitHub
  • Custom internal automation scripts using the GitHub API
  • Security tooling downloading rule/signature updates from GitHub
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pip.exe","npm.exe","go.exe","node.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the initiating binary — an unsigned or side-loaded host (python.exe from Temp, or a version.dll/wtsapi32.dll host) polling GitHub on a fixed cadence is the Matryoshka mailbox beacon; check the account adioziaete and repo memio if visible. 2) Contain: block GitHub egress for the offending process/host, isolate the endpoint. 3) Hunt: correlate the same host with the LNK/certutil chain, python311.dll side-load, and 45.158.196.184:8888; review per-host <computer>_<username> directories in the repo history if access is available.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.github.com","raw.githubusercontent.com","codeload.github.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("git.exe","code.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","gh.exe","curl.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","WindowsTerminal.exe","devenv.exe")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hits=count(), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl, 10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstHostname has_any ("api.github.com","raw.githubusercontent.com","codeload.github.com")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count() by DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationHostname:(api.github.com OR raw.githubusercontent.com OR codeload.github.com) -@Image:(*\git.exe OR *\Code.exe OR *\chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\firefox.exe OR *\gh.exe OR *\curl.exe OR *\powershell.exe)

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc

| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false

            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count

    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
