Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Marimo CVE-2026-39987 pre-auth RCE: marimo notebook process spawning a shell · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Chinese Hacker Commands DeepSeek via Telegram to Launch Autonomous Attacks
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Hermes/DeepSeek autonomous AI agent artifact: python3 -m http.server 8888 from /home/worker · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] NetScaler CVE-2026-3055 SAML IdP memory overread: high-volume /saml/login scraping
Hermes/DeepSeek autonomous AI agent artifact: python3 -m http.server 8888 from /home/worker AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the opsec-failure artifact that exposed this campaign: the Hermes Agent (DeepSeek-driven, 'Yolo' unattended mode) launched a Python stdlib file server on port 8888 out of /home/worker, exposing exploit scripts, API keys and session logs. This surfaces the same autonomous-agent tooling running on your own Linux fleet or on a compromised host being used as a staging box. Rationale: Uses the exact opsec artifact Unit 42 named — 'Hermes Agent exposed the operation by starting python3 -m http.server 8888 from /home/worker'. The http.server module + fixed port 8888 combination is the high-fidelity anchor; the /home/worker CWD / 'worker' account is projected as an enrichment flag. Cross-checked Unit 42 and BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hacker-uses-deepseek-ai-to-autonomously-attack-vulnerable-servers/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data scientist / developer running 'python -m http.server 8888' to quickly share files on a lab host
  • CI runner or container serving build artifacts over the stdlib http server on 8888
  • Internal documentation preview served with http.server on the conventional 8888 port
  • Ad-hoc troubleshooting of a Jupyter-adjacent workflow where 8888 is the habitual port
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountName in~ ("jenkins","gitlab-runner","builder") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bash","sh") and ProcessCommandLine has "/build/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree and shell history around the http.server PID — confirm the CWD and enumerate sibling processes (exploit scripts, curl/wget to FOFA/GitHub, other python agents). Check whether the parent is an interactive shell (benign dev) vs an unattended agent/cron. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the listener, and rotate any API keys/tokens present under the serving directory (Hermes exposed model API keys). 3) Hunt: on the same host look for outbound to FOFA/GitHub raw-content, downloaded public exploit files, and marimo/n8n/langflow scanning cmdlines; sweep the fleet for other :8888 http.server listeners.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("python","python3")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "http.server" and ProcessCommandLine has "8888"
| extend HermesHomeDir = (ProcessCommandLine has "/home/worker" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/home/worker" or AccountName =~ "worker")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, HermesHomeDir
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("python","python3")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "http.server" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "8888"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcess = ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Marimo CVE-2026-39987 pre-auth RCE: marimo notebook process spawning a shell AIExploitation High
Hunts successful exploitation of the Marimo unauthenticated /terminal/ws WebSocket flaw, where an attacker obtains a root PTY shell. Detection fires when the marimo notebook server process spawns an interactive shell or recon/download binary — the direct post-RCE landing that the agent used to run commands on 11 Marimo instances. Rationale: Corroborated via GitHub advisory GHSA-2679-6mx9-h9xc / Resecurity: the /terminal/ws endpoint skips validate_auth() and hands back a root PTY, so a marimo (python) parent spawning sh/bash/curl is the unambiguous RCE landing. Parent keyed on 'marimo' in cmdline/path; alternative web-log angle is a WebSocket upgrade to /terminal/ws. Datadog left empty — auditd parent-process correlation isn't expressible with the documented Datadog linux.auditd fields. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2679-6mx9-h9xc • https://www.resecurity.com/blog/article/marimo-pre-auth-rce-via-unauthenticated-websocket-terminal-cve-2026-39987 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/04/marimo-rce-flaw-cve-2026-39987.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate notebook code cells that shell out (subprocess/os.system) to run tooling as part of a data pipeline
  • Marimo admin running a terminal deliberately for maintenance
  • Container entrypoint scripts where marimo is the PID 1 wrapper spawning shell helpers on startup
  • CI job that launches marimo and immediately shells to install dependencies
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildProcess in~ ("python","python3") and ChildCmd has "pip install")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the child shell's command line and downstream activity (whoami/id showing root, curl/wget of second-stage payloads). Correlate with a web request to /terminal/ws around the same timestamp and check the source IP against the >460-target scanning infrastructure. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the marimo process and shell, and confirm Marimo is upgraded to >=0.23.0 (fixed build). 3) Hunt: pull all commands run via the PTY, look for persistence (cron, systemd, SSH keys), and sweep for other internet-exposed marimo/notebook interfaces still on vulnerable versions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "marimo" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "marimo" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "marimo"

NetScaler CVE-2026-3055 SAML IdP memory overread: high-volume /saml/login scraping AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts exploitation of the Citrix NetScaler SAML IdP memory-overread flaw used to exfiltrate data from three organizations. A single source repeatedly hits the SAML IdP /saml/login endpoint to leak leftover request memory (session tokens/data) — abnormal versus real users who authenticate once. Applies to customer-managed NetScaler ADC/Gateway configured as a SAML IdP. Rationale: Anchored on the corroborated exploitation primitive: Horizon3/watchTowr/Fortinet confirm CVE-2026-3055 is triggered by repeated requests to the SAML IdP '/saml/login' endpoint (NSC_TASS) to over-read appliance memory, and the article ties this to data exfil from three orgs. A single source hammering /saml/login 100+ times per 10m is the differentiator from legitimate single-shot SAML logins. Defender/Falcon/Datadog left empty — NetScaler appliance web telemetry lands in Sentinel CEF and web-proxy datamodels, not endpoint EDR; Sigma skipped because this is a volumetric/threshold detection. Cross-checked against: • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/vulnerabilities/cve-2026-3055/ • https://watchtowr.com/resources/rapid-reaction-to-cve-2026-3055/ • https://threat-modeling.com/citrix-netscaler-saml-idp-cve-2026-3055/
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A busy legitimate SAML IdP fronting many apps where a NAT/egress gateway concentrates hundreds of real logins behind one SourceIP
  • Uptime/synthetic monitoring repeatedly probing the /saml/login health path
  • Load-testing or SSO integration testing hammering the IdP endpoint
  • A misconfigured SP retry loop re-requesting /saml/login
Suppression filter
| where DistinctUA <= 2 and SourceIP !in ("<corporate_nat_egress_ip>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: profile the top SourceIP — is it a corporate NAT egress (many real users) or a single external/hosting-provider IP with one user-agent and no successful auth follow-through? Inspect response sizes/status for the over-read pattern. 2) Contain: block the source at the NetScaler/WAF, and verify the appliance is on the fixed build (14.1-66.59 / 13.1-62.23 or later); if unpatched and configured as SAML IdP, treat leaked session material as compromised and rotate. 3) Hunt: correlate the SourceIP against inbound access to Langflow/n8n/marimo scanning, and review authenticated sessions from tokens that may have been leaked from appliance memory.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor has "Citrix" or DeviceProduct has_any ("NetScaler","ADC")
| where RequestURL has "/saml/login"
| summarize Requests = count(), DistinctUA = dcount(RequestClientApplication), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), SampleURLs = make_set(RequestURL, 5) by SourceIP, DestinationHostName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where Requests > 100    // 100+ /saml/login hits from one source in 10m = memory scraping, not a real login
| order by Requests desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agents min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/saml/login*") by Web.src Web.dest _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where count > 100 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url

     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:

let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Network Anomaly Detection in KATA

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-07-31 6 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

An analysis of how Network Anomaly Detection (NAD) rules work within Kaspersky Anti Targeted Attack, using Kerberoasting and DNS tunneling attacks as examples.

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190 T1558 T1558.003
Domainstestinglab.ru crust.testinglab.ru

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DNS tunneling: host issuing many long unique subdomain queries under one parent domain · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains · DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Kerberoasting: single account/host requesting TGS tickets for many unique non-system SPNs
Kerberoasting: single account/host requesting TGS tickets for many unique non-system SPNs AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the exact anomaly the KATA NAD 'Signs of a Kerberoasting attack' rule targets: one client account (cname) from one source IP receiving successful Kerberos TGS responses for N or more distinct service (non-machine) SPNs inside a short window. System/computer-account SPNs are excluded because they carry uncrackable auto-generated passwords, mirroring the article's excl logic. Fan-out volume, not encryption type, is the signal. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact NAD logic — KRB_TGS_REP fan-out (dcount of non-'$' ServiceName per requesting cname/source IP) with system SPNs excluded and a count_spns threshold, rather than RC4 signature. MITRE DET0157 independently describes the same 'one account, many distinct SPNs, short window' pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/detectionstrategies/DET0157/ • https://securelist.com/tr/network-anomaly-detection-in-kata/120892/
ATT&CKT1558.003
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualys/BloodHound collectors) enumerating SPNs across the domain
  • SCCM/MECM or monitoring service accounts that legitimately touch many services at startup
  • A privileged admin workstation opening many Kerberos-authenticated apps (SQL, CIFS, HTTP) in a burst after logon
  • Backup/inventory tooling that iterates service accounts
  • Login storms after a DC reboot causing batched ticket requests
Suppression filter
| where TargetUserName !in~ ("svc-scanner","svc-bloodhound","svc-sccm") and IpAddress !in ("10.0.0.0/8-scanner-subnet")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot on TargetUserName + IpAddress; resolve the source host and confirm whether the account/host normally requests these SPNs. Check if requests came from a workstation vs a server and whether the targeted accounts are high-value (SQL/admin service accounts). 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, disable/force-reset the requesting account and any targeted service-account passwords (assume offline crack in progress), and isolate the source host. 3) Hunt: search for the same source IP performing LDAP SPN enumeration prior to the burst, subsequent logons using the targeted service accounts, and Rubeus/Impacket GetUserSPNs command-line artifacts on the source host.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where EventID == 4769
| where Status == "0x0"                       // successful TGS-REP only (article: KRB_TGS_REP)
| where ServiceName !endswith "$"             // exclude machine/computer-account SPNs (auto-generated strong passwords)
| where ServiceName !in~ ("krbtgt")
| where TargetUserName !endswith "$" and TargetUserName !in~ ("","-")
| summarize UniqueSPNs = dcount(ServiceName), TargetedSPNs = make_set(ServiceName, 25), TGSRequests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by TargetUserName, IpAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where UniqueSPNs >= 10           // count_spns threshold: single account pulling >=10 distinct service SPNs in 10m
| order by UniqueSPNs desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4769 -@TargetUserName:*$
ENDPOINT
`wineventlog_security` EventCode=4769 Service_Name!="*$" Service_Name!="krbtgt" Account_Name!="*$" Failure_Code="0x0"
| eval win=bin(_time, span=10m)
| stats dc(Service_Name) AS unique_spns values(Service_Name) AS targeted_spns count AS tgs_requests min(_time) AS firstTime max(_time) AS lastTime by Account_Name, Client_Address, win
| where unique_spns >= 10
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - unique_spns
DNS tunneling: host issuing many long unique subdomain queries under one parent domain AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the KATA 'Data tunneling in DNS traffic' anomaly: a single host emitting a high volume of unique, abnormally long subdomain labels under one parent zone (encoded data smuggled in the QNAME). Behaviour-based — thresholds on unique-subdomain count and label length rather than a static domain IOC — so it catches the article's example (e.g. crust.testinglab.ru-style beacons) and unknown tunnels alike. Rationale: Anchors on the article's KATA rule shape — per-source high volume of unique subdomains under a single parent zone, with long QNAMEs carrying encoded data — instead of the disposable lab IOC (testinglab.ru / crust.testinglab.ru is a Kaspersky test zone, not shipped as an IOC). MITRE DET0400 corroborates the long-label (>30 char) + abnormal query-volume-to-single-domain signals; thresholds set at 40-char avg / 50 unique labels. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/detectionstrategies/DET0400/ • https://securelist.com/tr/network-anomaly-detection-in-kata/120892/
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CDN / anti-bot providers (Akamai, Cloudflare, CDN edge tokens) that embed long hashed labels in FQDNs
  • Antivirus/EDR cloud-reputation lookups that hash file/URL data into subdomains (e.g. McAfee, Sophos, Trend)
  • Telemetry/analytics SDKs beaconing device IDs as subdomain labels
  • Email security gateways doing SPF/DKIM/DMARC and RBL lookups in bulk
  • Legitimate DNS-based licensing or software-update check-ins with encoded tokens
Suppression filter
| where Parent !endswith "akamaiedge.net" and Parent !endswith "cloudflare.com" and Parent !endswith "trafficmanager.net" and Parent !endswith "amazonaws.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent zone and the initiating process/host; check domain age/registration and whether the zone is a known CDN/security vendor. Inspect sample QNAMEs for base32/base64/hex encoding and consistent length. 2) Contain: if the zone is unrecognised, sinkhole/block it at the resolver and isolate the source host; capture the process making the queries. 3) Hunt: pivot to other hosts querying the same parent zone, correlate to a non-browser/non-system parent process (powershell/rundll32/python) initiating the DNS, and look for matching TXT/NULL/CNAME record types indicative of a tunnel utility (iodine, dnscat2).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend Labels = split(RemoteUrl, ".")
| where array_length(Labels) >= 3
| extend Parent = strcat(tostring(Labels[array_length(Labels)-2]), ".", tostring(Labels[array_length(Labels)-1]))
| where Parent !endswith "in-addr.arpa"
| summarize UniqueFqdns = dcount(RemoteUrl), AvgLen = avg(strlen(RemoteUrl)), MaxLen = max(strlen(RemoteUrl)), Conns = count(), Sample = make_set(RemoteUrl, 10)
    by DeviceName, Parent, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where UniqueFqdns >= 50 and AvgLen >= 40    // 50 distinct long labels under one zone in 10m = tunneling shape
| order by UniqueFqdns desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where isnotempty(Name)
| where Name !endswith ".in-addr.arpa" and Name !endswith ".arpa"
| extend Labels = split(Name, ".")
| where array_length(Labels) >= 3
| extend Parent = strcat(tostring(Labels[array_length(Labels)-2]), ".", tostring(Labels[array_length(Labels)-1]))
| extend TopLabelLen = strlen(tostring(Labels[0]))
| summarize UniqueSubdomains = dcount(Name), QueryCount = count(), AvgLen = avg(strlen(Name)), MaxTopLabel = max(TopLabelLen), Sample = make_set(Name, 10)
    by ClientIP, Parent, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where UniqueSubdomains >= 50 and AvgLen >= 40   // MITRE DET0400: many long unique labels to one zone
| order by UniqueSubdomains desc
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/.{40,}/
| regex("(?<parent>[a-z0-9-]+\.[a-z]+)$", field=DomainName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, parent], function=[count(field=DomainName, distinct=true, as=unique_long_subdomains), count(as=total_queries)])
| unique_long_subdomains >= 50
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count AS query_count, dc(DNS.query) AS unique_subdomains, values(DNS.query) AS sample_queries FROM datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS WHERE nodename=DNS DNS.message_type="QUERY" BY DNS.src, DNS.query, _time span=10m
| eval parent=replace(DNS.query, "^.*?\.([^.]+\.[^.]+)$", "\1"), qlen=len(DNS.query)
| stats sum(query_count) AS total_queries, dc(DNS.query) AS unique_subdomains, avg(qlen) AS avg_len, max(qlen) AS max_len, values(sample_queries) AS sample_queries BY DNS.src, parent
| where unique_subdomains >= 50 AND avg_len >= 40
| sort - unique_subdomains
| tstats summariesonly=false count AS query_count, dc(DNS.query) AS unique_subdomains, values(DNS.query) AS sample_queries FROM datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS WHERE nodename=DNS DNS.message_type="QUERY" BY DNS.src, DNS.query, _time span=10m
| eval parent=replace(DNS.query, "^.*?\.([^.]+\.[^.]+)$", "\1"), qlen=len(DNS.query)
| stats sum(query_count) AS total_queries, dc(DNS.query) AS unique_subdomains, avg(qlen) AS avg_len, max(qlen) AS max_len, values(sample_queries) AS sample_queries BY DNS.src, parent
| where unique_subdomains >= 50 AND avg_len >= 40
| sort - unique_subdomains
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest

XCSSET v40 CDP hijack: Google Chrome launched with remote-debugging-port AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the XCSSET v40 Chrome-hijacking module activating the Chrome DevTools Protocol by relaunching the legitimate Google Chrome binary with --remote-debugging-port (and, post-Chrome-136, a non-default --user-data-dir) so the dropped chrome_remote binary can attach to the browser engine. Article-specific because it targets the exact CDP-enablement command line the wrapper uses on the real Chrome binary, not headless automation. Rationale: Uses the article's exact CDP-enablement behaviour (legitimate 'Google Chrome' binary + --remote-debugging-port, with --user-data-dir surfaced because Chrome 136+ ignores the switch on the default profile). Cross-checked against MITRE S0658 and vendor write-ups confirming the CDP module. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0658/ • https://www.securityweek.com/new-xcsset-macos-malware-variant-hijacks-cryptocurrency-transactions/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/09/new-macos-xcsset-variant-targets.html
ATT&CKT1185 T1539 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers running Selenium/Puppeteer/Playwright test suites that launch Chrome with a debugging port
  • chromedriver-driven CI/automation on developer laptops
  • Manual QA using `--remote-debugging-port` for front-end debugging
  • VS Code / JS debugger 'attach to Chrome' launch configs
  • Lighthouse / performance-profiling tooling launching Chrome with CDP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chromedriver","node","python","python3","Code Helper") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "puppeteer" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "selenium"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the launching parent — automation binaries (chromedriver/node/python) are benign; a shell, osascript, or unknown wrapper parenting real 'Google Chrome' with a debugging port is suspicious. Check for a chrome_remote binary or a 'boot' process on the same host in the same window. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the Chrome + chrome_remote processes, and force-revoke/rotate browser session cookies and any SSO tokens (CDP theft is invisible to the user). 3) Hunt: pivot to all Xcode projects on the host for injected loader scripts, look for the C2 URI paths (/s/, /d/, /l, /u) in proxy logs, and check other developer endpoints that cloned the same repo.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "Google Chrome"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chromedriver","node","python","python3")
| extend UsesCustomProfile = iff(ProcessCommandLine has "--user-data-dir", "yes", "no")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ParentProcess=InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, UsesCustomProfile, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has "Google Chrome"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ActingProcessName !has "chromedriver" and ActingProcessName !has "node" and ActingProcessName !has "python"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

XCSSET v40 chrome_remote backdoor execution and C2 WebSocket egress AICommand & Control High
Hunts the dropped chrome_remote Mach-O binary that XCSSET v40 uses to attach to the opened CDP port and open a persistent WebSocket to the rotating C2 for real-time JavaScript injection and cookie exfiltration. High fidelity because chrome_remote is a unique, article-named binary that should never exist on a clean macOS host. Rationale: Pivots on the article's uniquely named chrome_remote binary (the CDP-attach/WebSocket-C2 component) — a name absent from any legitimate macOS install, giving a low-FP, high-confidence signal. Corroborated by MITRE S0658 and vendor reporting describing the CDP cookie-theft backdoor. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0658/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/ • https://www.securityweek.com/new-xcsset-macos-malware-variant-hijacks-cryptocurrency-transactions/
ATT&CKT1185 T1071.001 T1539 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Extremely rare — no legitimate macOS software ships a binary named chrome_remote
  • A developer's own project artifact coincidentally named chrome_remote (check code-signing/notarization and path)
  • Security researcher detonating XCSSET samples in a lab
  • An unrelated 'Chrome Remote Desktop' component (verify full path/signature — the real one is 'chrome-remote-desktop', not 'chrome_remote')
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the chrome_remote path and SHA256, verify it is unsigned/un-notarized and dropped outside a normal app bundle; confirm whether it made outbound connections and to which host. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, terminate chrome_remote and its parent Chrome, block the resolved C2 IP/domain at the proxy, and invalidate all browser sessions and OAuth tokens for the user. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for the same SHA256, for Chrome launched with --remote-debugging-port (UC1), and for infected Xcode projects/loader scripts that would re-drop the binary on the next build.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "chrome_remote" or FolderPath endswith "/chrome_remote"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ParentProcess=InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has "chrome_remote"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

XCSSET v40 build-triggered loader: Xcode build spawning osascript/curl AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the XCSSET v40 initial infection that fires only when a developer builds an infected Xcode project locally — the injected loader runs from an Xcode Run-Script build phase and spawns osascript or curl to reach the C2 and stage further modules. Article-specific because it targets the Xcode/xcodebuild build-tree ancestry that is XCSSET's signature delivery vector. Rationale: Grounded in the article's core delivery mechanic — infection triggers when the developer builds the infected Xcode project, with an AppleScript/curl loader establishing C2. Ancestry on xcodebuild/Xcode + osascript/curl is XCSSET-specific and distinct from generic script execution. Cross-checked against MITRE S0658. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0658/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/09/new-macos-xcsset-variant-targets.html
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CocoaPods / Swift Package Manager or fastlane Run-Script phases that curl dependencies during a build
  • SwiftLint / build scripts using osascript to post notifications or display dialogs
  • In-house build automation that pings a webhook via curl on build completion
  • Crashlytics/Sentry dSYM upload scripts invoking curl from a build phase
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cocoapods","github.com","swiftpm","fastlane","crashlytics","sentry-cli"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the ProcessCommandLine of the osascript/curl child — benign build tooling references known package hosts (cocoapods.org, github.com dependency URLs); XCSSET reaches short single-letter C2 paths (/a, /s/, /d/) and base64 payloads. Inspect the offending Xcode project's build phases for an injected script. 2) Contain: quarantine the project/repo, isolate the endpoint if C2 contact is confirmed, and block the destination host. 3) Hunt: check whether Chrome was subsequently launched with --remote-debugging-port (UC1) or chrome_remote executed (UC2), and identify every other developer who cloned/built the same repo to scope worming across projects.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("osascript","curl")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("xcodebuild","Xcode")
    or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("xcodebuild","Xcode")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (".xcodeproj",".xcworkspace","DerivedData","Build/Intermediates.noindex")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, Parent=InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, GrandParent=InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("osascript","curl")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("xcodebuild","Xcode") or ParentProcessName has_any ("xcodebuild","Xcode") or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (".xcodeproj",".xcworkspace","DerivedData")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

TeamCity On-Premises server (java/Tomcat) spawning OS command interpreter — CVE-2026-63077 RCE AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation footprint of CVE-2026-63077: the TeamCity On-Premises server process (its bundled JRE / Tomcat catalina java process) spawning cmd/powershell/bash/discovery LOLBins. Builds run on agents, never on the server, so the server java process launching an OS shell is a high-fidelity RCE signal. Explicitly excludes the co-located build-agent process to avoid legitimate build-step noise. Rationale: Anchors on the article's confirmed mechanic — CVE-2026-63077 executes 'arbitrary OS commands with the privileges of the server process' via the agent polling protocol — by matching the TeamCity server's bundled java/catalina parent (cmdline contains TeamCity) spawning shells/LOLBins, while excluding buildAgent since legitimate build steps run on agents not the server. Cross-checked JetBrains advisory, Rapid7, Help Net Security and The Hacker News. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.jetbrains.com/teamcity/2026/07/cve-2026-63077/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-63077-critical-unauthenticated-remote-code-execution-in-jetbrains-teamcity/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/28/teamcity-rce-cve-2026-63077-fixed/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/critical-teamcity-flaw-could-let.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TeamCity server and build agent installed on the same host, where the agent's java process runs build steps that shell out (mitigated by the buildAgent exclusion)
  • Sysadmin running diagnostic commands under the TeamCity service account on the server host
  • Server-side VCS/plugin tooling that legitimately shells out (rare; typically git.exe/svn.exe which are not in the child list)
  • Monitoring/backup agents invoked via the Tomcat service wrapper
  • Custom server-side health-check scripts launched from teamcity-server.bat startup
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "buildAgent" and not (FileName =~ "cmd.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("teamcity-server.bat","runAll.bat","service.bat","wrapper"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the parent is the TeamCity SERVER java process (cmdline has TeamCity + catalina/Bootstrap and NOT buildAgent) and inspect the child command line for recon (whoami/net/nltest) or download (certutil/curl) intent; capture SHA256 and check TeamCity server version against 2025.11.7 / 2026.1.3. 2) Contain: Network-isolate the TeamCity host, rotate all credentials stored in TeamCity (VCS tokens, cloud keys, artifact-repo creds — assume exposed per advisory), and take the server offline from the internet. 3) Hunt: Pivot on the host for outbound C2 from the java/child process, new admin users or tokens in TeamCity, tampered build configs/artifacts, and repeat the query across all TeamCity server hosts for lateral spread.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","tomcat9.exe","java")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "TeamCity"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("catalina","Bootstrap","teamcity-server")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "buildAgent"   // builds run on the AGENT, not the server
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh","bash","whoami.exe","whoami","net.exe","net1.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bitsadmin.exe","nltest.exe","ipconfig.exe","hostname.exe","reg.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has "java"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "TeamCity"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("catalina","Bootstrap","teamcity-server")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has "buildAgent"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash","sh","whoami","net.exe","net1.exe","certutil.exe","curl","wget","bitsadmin.exe","nltest.exe","reg.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentImage = ActingProcessName, ParentCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = TargetProcessName, ChildCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TeamCity Server Process Spawning OS Command Interpreter (CVE-2026-63077 RCE)
id: b3d9f0a2-1c4e-4a7b-9e21-7f2c6a8d5e10
status: experimental
description: Detects the TeamCity On-Premises server (bundled JRE / Tomcat java) spawning an OS shell or discovery LOLBin, the post-exploitation footprint of the CVE-2026-63077 unauthenticated deserialization RCE. Builds execute on agents, so the server java process launching a shell is anomalous.
references:
  - https://blog.jetbrains.com/teamcity/2026/07/cve-2026-63077/

tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059

logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\java.exe'
      - '\javaw.exe'

    ParentCommandLine|contains: 'TeamCity'

    Image|endswith:

  - Server-side maintenance tooling invoked via the service wrapper
level: high

Unpatched internet-facing TeamCity On-Premises exposed to CVE-2026-63077 AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces TeamCity On-Premises hosts still exposed to CVE-2026-63077 (all versions below 2025.11.7 / 2026.1.3), prioritising internet-facing servers. Because the flaw is unauthenticated and CVSS 9.8, exposure inventory is the fastest path to shrinking the attack surface before exploitation. Article-specific: keys directly on the CVE ID and vendor-named fixed versions. Rationale: Uses the two article-confirmed facts — CVE-2026-63077 and the fixed versions 2025.11.7 / 2026.1.3 with 'all versions affected' — to enumerate exposed TeamCity servers, joining DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing to prioritise the unauthenticated-HTTP attack path the advisory calls out. Verified against JetBrains, Rapid7, and SecurityWeek. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.jetbrains.com/teamcity/2026/07/cve-2026-63077/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-63077-critical-unauthenticated-remote-code-execution-in-jetbrains-teamcity/ • https://www.securityweek.com/critical-code-execution-vulnerability-patched-in-teamcity/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Server already patched via the security-patch plugin but TVM still keys on the base version number (plugin patches without version bump — verify plugin install state)
  • TeamCity Cloud agents mislabeled as On-Premises (Cloud is not affected per advisory)
  • Decommissioned/offline TeamCity hosts still present in the vuln inventory
  • Non-production/lab TeamCity instances on isolated segments flagged as internet-facing by stale network data
  • TVM version-detection lag immediately after an in-progress upgrade to 2025.11.7 / 2026.1.3
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareName has "TeamCity" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "2025.11.7" and SoftwareVersion !startswith "2026.1.3"
Response runbook
1) Triage: Rank hits by IsInternetFacing=true, then confirm each host's TeamCity version and whether the CVE-2026-63077 security-patch plugin is installed (plugin fixes without a version bump, so cross-check plugin state, not just version string). 2) Contain: For any internet-facing unpatched server, place it behind VPN/WAF or restrict the login page + REST API by source IP immediately (per JetBrains best-practice guidance) and schedule emergency upgrade to 2025.11.7 or 2026.1.3. 3) Hunt: On every exposed host, run the companion RCE detection (server java spawning a shell) over the exposure window and review TeamCity audit logs / stored-credential access for signs the flaw was already exploited before patching.

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Vulnerable @aws-amplify/codegen-ui-react (<=2.20.2) present on endpoints/build hosts (CVE-2025-4318)
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] AWS Amplify UI Builder CreateComponent/UpdateComponent carrying JS expression payload (CVE-2025-4318)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Amplify codegen (node) process spawning shell/LOLBin child — CVE-2025-4318 build-time RCE

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
AWS Amplify UI Builder CreateComponent/UpdateComponent carrying JS expression payload (CVE-2025-4318) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts CloudTrail CreateComponent/UpdateComponent calls to the amplifyuibuilder service whose component-schema request body contains raw JavaScript expression tokens (require(, child_process, process.env, eval(, constructor, ${). CVE-2025-4318 lets an authenticated user plant such an expression in a component property binding, which the amplify-codegen-ui expression-binding function evaluates as arbitrary JS at render/build time. Rationale: Pivots on the exact article-named API surface (amplifyuibuilder CreateComponent/UpdateComponent, the create-component vector) plus JS tokens that only appear when a component property binding is being weaponised as an expression per CVE-2025-4318. CloudTrail is the only telemetry that captures the plant regardless of where the build runs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hf3j-86p7-mfw8 • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2025-4318/ • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amplifyuibuilder/latest/APIReference/API_CreateComponent.html • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amplify/latest/userguide/logging-using-cloudtrail.html
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1078
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developers authoring components with binding expressions that happen to reference 'constructor' or template literals '${...}' in labels/text
  • IaC/CI automation that programmatically calls CreateComponent/UpdateComponent with generated schemas
  • Amplify Studio Figma-to-code imports that embed complex property bindings
  • Component names or field labels literally containing the word 'eval' or 'process'
Suppression filter
| where NOT match(object,"(?i)^(test|demo|sample)")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full CloudTrail record and inspect requestParameters.componentToCreate (bindingProperties/collectionProperties/properties) for JS that reaches host APIs (require, child_process, process, fetch) — a benign UI expression never needs those. Note the calling principal (userIdentity.arn) and sourceIPAddress. 2) Contain: if malicious, delete the component, suspend/rotate the caller's credentials, and pin amplify-codegen-ui to >=2.20.4 in every app and CI pipeline so the payload cannot be re-evaluated. 3) Hunt: enumerate all CreateComponent/UpdateComponent by that principal across apps/regions and correlate with UC3 (build hosts spawning shells) and CodeBuild/Amplify build logs around the same window.

Vulnerable @aws-amplify/codegen-ui-react (<=2.20.2) present on endpoints/build hosts (CVE-2025-4318) AIWeaponization Medium
Surfaces hosts still carrying the vulnerable amplify-codegen-ui package (@aws-amplify/codegen-ui-react <= 2.20.2 / CVE-2025-4318) so they can be upgraded to 2.20.4 before an unsafe component expression is ever evaluated. Exposure hunt tied to the exact CVE and package name from the advisory. Rationale: Uses the CVE id and the concrete npm package name from the advisory. TVM CveId is the cleanest exposure signal; the Falcon FileWritten path catches installs of the vulnerable module where TVM npm coverage is thin. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hf3j-86p7-mfw8 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@aws-amplify/codegen-ui-react/CVE-2025-4318/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2025-4318/

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • TVM reporting a transitive copy already superseded by a patched top-level dependency
  • Air-gapped/offline build hosts where upgrade is deliberately deferred

1) Triage: confirm the installed SoftwareVersion is <= 2.20.2 and identify whether the host renders/builds externally-supplied component schemas (higher priority than local-only dev). 2) Contain: upgrade @aws-amplify/codegen-ui-react to 2.20.4 across app repos and CI images; rebuild artifacts generated by the vulnerable version. 3) Hunt: cross-reference these hosts against UC3 (amplify build spawning shells) and UC1 (who created components consumed by these hosts) to find any exploitation that already occurred.

Amplify codegen (node) process spawning shell/LOLBin child — CVE-2025-4318 build-time RCE AIExploitation Medium
Detects the arbitrary-JavaScript execution primitive of CVE-2025-4318 firing at build/render time: a node/npm process running the Amplify CLI or codegen (command line references amplify/codegen-ui) spawns a shell or LOLBin child. Legitimate component rendering never shells out; this is the malicious expression executing during the generate/build process. Rationale: Ties the article's 'arbitrary JavaScript during component rendering and build' to a concrete parent(node running amplify/codegen)->child(shell/LOLBin) tree. The amplify/codegen command-line predicate on the parent is what scopes this to CVE-2025-4318 rather than generic build-tool noise. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hf3j-86p7-mfw8 • https://blog.securelayer7.net/cve-2025-4318-aws-amplify-rce/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/critical-aws-amplify-studio-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Amplify/npm postinstall or codegen hooks that legitimately call a shell (git, sh -c) as part of the build
  • Custom Amplify overrides/transformers that shell out to helper scripts
  • CI runners where node wraps every step and spawns bash for lifecycle scripts
  • Developer running 'amplify codegen' then chaining a shell in the same wrapper script
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","bash.exe","bash","sh") and (ProcessCommandLine has "amplify-cli" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("git ","rev-parse","lifecycle")))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the parent InitiatingProcessCommandLine (confirm amplify/codegen) and the child ProcessCommandLine — a spawn that fetches (curl/certutil), writes to disk, or launches an interpreter with an inline payload is a true positive; a plain 'sh -c' lifecycle hook usually is not. 2) Contain: isolate the build host/runner, kill the child process tree, and revoke any cloud credentials that node had in its environment (build hosts often hold deploy keys). 3) Hunt: pivot on the child's SHA256 and any RemoteUrl/RemoteIP it contacted, and back-trace to the component (UC1) and package version (UC2) that seeded the execution.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.cmd","npx.cmd","yarn.cmd","pnpm.cmd")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("amplify","codegen-ui","amplifyuibuilder","codegen")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","bash","sh","zsh","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe")

| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash","sh","zsh","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

StepSecurity

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Compromised @joyfill npm bundle dropped in node_modules (2773 beta RAT)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Compromised npm Packages: @joyfill/components and @joyfill/layouts Ship an Obfus
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Node.js spawning detached 'node -e' second-stage child (/$/boot loader) · [LLM] @joyfill RAT persistence: Node rewriting VS Code / Discord / GitHub Desktop / npm modules · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] @joyfill RAT C2 callout to hardcoded IPs / Socket.IO boot paths · [LLM] Node.js resolving C2 via blockchain dead-drop (Tron/BSC/Aptos RPC) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Compromised @joyfill npm bundle dropped in node_modules (2773 beta RAT) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for the malicious @joyfill/components or @joyfill/layouts distribution bundles landing on disk under node_modules, matched by the article's payload SHA256 hashes and the exact dist file paths the RAT was injected into. Catches the supply-chain implant at install/checkout time on developer machines, CI runners, and repos. Rationale: Anchored on the three payload SHA256 hashes and the exact injected bundles named in the article (dist/index.js, index.esm.js, joyfill.min.js, index.cjs.js, index.es.js) under @joyfill node_modules — no legitimate release ships these hashes. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/joyfill-npm-supply-chain-compromise • https://socket.dev/blog/polinrider-north-korea-linked-supply-chain-campaign-expands • https://research.jfrog.com/post/hijacked-npm-vscode-tasks-blockchain/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer intentionally re-pinning to a clean @joyfill release (path matches but hash will not)
  • Internal artifact-mirror caching legitimate pre-July-28 @joyfill tarballs
  • Security team restoring the malicious sample into a sandbox for analysis
  • EDR re-scanning an existing node_modules tree during a full disk sweep
Suppression filter
| where not (isnotempty(SHA256) and SHA256 !in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18","36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c","cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the SHA256 and file path — if hash matches, it is the confirmed implant; if only path matches, diff the bundle for the `9-0135-3` marker string. Identify the device (dev workstation vs CI runner). 2. Contain: isolate the host, kill node processes, and remove the 2773-beta versions; force re-pin to a @joyfill release published before 2026-07-28. 3. Hunt: pivot on the host for outbound to the C2 IPs (166.88.134.62 / 23.27.13.43 / 198.105.127.210 / 23.27.202.27), node -e children, and modified @vscode/deviceid, Discord, GitHub Desktop, or npm CLI modules; rotate every credential present on the machine.

@joyfill RAT C2 callout to hardcoded IPs / Socket.IO boot paths AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound connections from developer/CI hosts to the four C2 IPs used by the @joyfill implant and to its distinctive request paths (/$/boot, /u/e, /u/f, /0x/js, /verify-human/, /snv). This is the Socket.IO RAT channel and the second-stage /$/boot downloader described in the article. Rationale: Uses the four verbatim C2 IPs and the six exact RAT request paths from the article's IOC block; these are static infrastructure indicators with essentially no benign use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/joyfill-npm-supply-chain-compromise • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/seven-malicious-vite-npm-packages-use.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.All_Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel scanner or sandbox deliberately probing the C2 IPs from a research host
  • Shared-hosting reuse: another benign service later assigned to 198.105.127.210 / 23.27.x ranges
  • A pentest replaying these IOCs during an authorized supply-chain exercise
  • Proxy log noise where /snv or /u/f appears in an unrelated legitimate API path (mitigated by pairing with the IPs)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","electron.exe","Code.exe","Cursor.exe") or RemoteIP in ("166.88.134.62","23.27.13.43","198.105.127.210","23.27.202.27")
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the initiating process is node.exe (or a dev tool bundling Node) and whether the destination is one of the four hardcoded IPs vs only a path match. 2. Contain: block the four C2 IPs at the egress proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and terminate Node processes. 3. Hunt: correlate with @joyfill bundle presence (UC1), node -e children hitting /$/boot, and outbound to the blockchain resolver hosts; treat all workstation credentials/tokens as exposed and rotate.

Node.js resolving C2 via blockchain dead-drop (Tron/BSC/Aptos RPC) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts for a Node.js process on a workstation or CI runner reaching public blockchain RPC endpoints (api.trongrid.io, bsc-dataseed.binance.org, bsc-rpc.publicnode.com, fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com) — the @joyfill implant's dead-drop resolver that reads a Tron transaction and follows it to a BSC transaction to decode its live C2. Blockchain RPC from a build/dev Node process is highly abnormal. Rationale: Uses the exact blockchain RPC hostnames named in the article's lookup-endpoint IOCs, scoped to a Node.js initiating process so legitimate wallet/crypto apps on the same host don't fire. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/joyfill-npm-supply-chain-compromise • https://research.jfrog.com/post/hijacked-npm-vscode-tasks-blockchain/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/seven-malicious-vite-npm-packages-use.html
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately building or testing a web3/dApp project that uses trongrid or bsc-dataseed via Node
  • CI job running blockchain integration tests against public RPC endpoints
  • A crypto-price widget or wallet SDK bundled into an Electron dev tool making these lookups
  • Corporate proxy collapsing the initiating process so node scoping is lost (widen review manually)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("hardhat","truffle","web3","ethers","@tronweb","foundry") )
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the Node process is not part of a known web3 project in that repo — check the working directory / command line and the presence of @joyfill in node_modules. 2. Contain: if @joyfill or the C2 IPs are also present, isolate the host and kill node; otherwise annotate as likely-benign web3 dev. 3. Hunt: look for the follow-on eval-based execution and outbound to the four C2 IPs on the same host within minutes of the RPC lookup.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.trongrid.io","fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com","bsc-dataseed.binance.org","bsc-rpc.publicnode.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("api.trongrid.io","fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com","bsc-dataseed.binance.org","bsc-rpc.publicnode.com")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js spawning detached 'node -e' second-stage child (/$/boot loader) AIInstallation Medium
Detects a node.exe process spawning another node.exe with an inline `-e` script — the @joyfill implant's detached second stage that requests /$/boot from a second host and XOR-decrypts the response, running independently of the Socket.IO channel. Inline eval children of Node are rare on developer endpoints. Rationale: Targets the article's described 'detached node -e child that requests /$/boot' — the node→node -e parent/child shape plus the /$/boot path is a specific behavioural fingerprint, not a generic Node launch. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/joyfill-npm-supply-chain-compromise
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Build tooling (webpack/vite/jest workers) that legitimately forks node with -e for worker bootstrapping
  • nvm / npx wrapper scripts invoking node --eval
  • Monorepo task runners (turbo, nx) spawning inline-eval node helpers
  • A developer manually running node -e for a quick one-liner
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("webpack","vite","jest-worker","turbo","nx","ts-node","npx") and not ProcessCommandLine has "/$/boot")
Response runbook
1. Triage: read the child's full command line — a genuine build worker will reference a project path; the implant references /$/boot or an opaque XOR/eval blob. 2. Contain: if the command line contains /$/boot or unreadable eval content, isolate the host and kill both node processes. 3. Hunt: check the same host for @joyfill bundles, blockchain RPC lookups, and outbound to 23.27.13.43 (the /$/boot server); rotate credentials.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe" and FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (" -e ","--eval") or ProcessCommandLine has "/$/boot"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessId, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has "node.exe" and ActingProcessName has "node.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (" -e ","--eval") or ActingProcessCommandLine has "/$/boot"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())

@joyfill RAT persistence: Node rewriting VS Code / Discord / GitHub Desktop / npm modules AIInstallation High
Detects node.exe modifying the developer-tool modules the @joyfill implant hijacks for persistence — @vscode/deviceid (used by VS Code, Cursor, Antigravity), the Discord desktop core module, GitHub Desktop main.js, and the global npm CLI — into which it inserts a self-reloading block. These files are not normally rewritten by a Node process. Rationale: Directly enumerates the four persistence targets named in the article (@vscode/deviceid, Discord desktop core, GitHub Desktop main.js, global npm CLI) and requires a node/npm writer — legitimate installers use msiexec/updater processes, not node rewriting these in place. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/joyfill-npm-supply-chain-compromise • https://research.jfrog.com/post/hijacked-npm-vscode-tasks-blockchain/ • https://socket.dev/blog/polinrider-north-korea-linked-supply-chain-campaign-expands
ATT&CKT1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate `npm install -g` upgrading the global npm CLI (writes npm-cli.js via node)
  • VS Code / Cursor auto-update rewriting bundled @vscode/deviceid
  • Discord client self-update repackaging discord_desktop_core
  • GitHub Desktop applying its own squirrel auto-update to main.js
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install -g","npm-upgrade","update-notifier") and FileName =~ "npm-cli.js")
Response runbook
1. Triage: inspect the modifying node/npm command line and diff the touched module for an injected self-reloading block or the `9-0135-3` marker; a legit updater will be an official installer/updater process chain, not an ad-hoc node from a project dir. 2. Contain: isolate the host, kill node, and restore the affected modules from a clean install of VS Code/Discord/GitHub Desktop/npm. 3. Hunt: pivot to @joyfill bundle presence, C2 IP callouts, and the Python stealer's collection of browser/wallet/Git credentials; rotate all developer credentials and tokens on the host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| where FolderPath has @"\@vscode\deviceid\"
     or FolderPath has "discord_desktop_core"
     or (FolderPath has "GitHub Desktop" and FileName =~ "main.js")
     or FileName =~ "npm-cli.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\@vscode\deviceid\"
     or TargetFilePath has "discord_desktop_core"
     or (TargetFilePath has "GitHub Desktop" and TargetFileName =~ "main.js")
     or TargetFileName =~ "npm-cli.js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: @joyfill implant persistence via developer-tool module rewrite
id: 6a1b3d27-8f4e-4c90-a2d5-9e0c7b1f5a63
description: node.exe or npm.exe modifying @vscode/deviceid, Discord core, GitHub Desktop main.js, or npm-cli.js for self-reloading persistence
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/29
tags:

logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
